diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable progressive hemodynamic disease driven by neurohormonal activation (RAAS and sympathetic nervous system).
whoIsAtRisk: Adults aged 60 and older with a history of hypertension or prior heart attack
People with long-standing diabetes, sleep apnea, or metabolic syndrome
Patients with chronic kidney disease (cardiorenal syndrome)
howToReduceRisk: Strictly restrict dietary sodium intake to under 2,000 mg daily
Weigh yourself every morning after urination to monitor sudden fluid retention
Adhere strictly to prescribed SGLT2 inhibitors, ARNI / ACEi, and beta-blockers
Avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) which cause fluid retention
whenToSeeDoctor: Sudden increase in weight of more than 3 lbs in a day or 5 lbs in a week
Worsening shortness of breath requiring multiple pillows to sleep at night
Severe sudden chest tightness, irregular racing pulse, or fainting
Progressive abdominal fullness, loss of appetite, or persistent nausea
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects over 64 million people worldwide, with prevalence increasing rapidly due to aging populations.
reliableSources: Heart Failure Society of America (HFSA) / ACC / AHA Guidelines
European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Heart Failure Guidelines
National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)

diseases.name: Atrial Fibrillation
diseases.shortDescription: An irregular and often very rapid heartbeat that can lead to blood clots, stroke, and heart failure.
diseases.whatIsIt: Atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia. During AFib, the heart’s upper chambers (atria) beat chaotically and out of coordination with the lower chambers (ventricles), causing blood to pool in the left atrial appendage where embolic clots can form.
whyDoesItHappen: Chronic hypertension causing structural remodeling and stretching of the left atrium
Coronary artery disease, prior heart surgery, or heart valve defects
Hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid) accelerating cardiac electrical conduction
Obstructive sleep apnea causing intermittent nocturnal hypoxemia and atrial strain
High alcohol intake (holiday heart syndrome), heavy caffeine, or acute infection
signsYouMayNotice: Sensations of a racing, flip-flopping, or pounding heartbeat (palpitations)
Unexplained dizziness, lightheadedness, or feeling faint upon standing
Noticeable reduction in exercise stamina and sudden breathlessness
Mild chest discomfort, pressure, or fluttering sensation
Extreme generalized fatigue during routine daytime activities
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable cardiac electrophysiological disorder involving electrical micro-reentry circuits in pulmonary vein antra.
whoIsAtRisk: Individuals aged 65 and older
People with high blood pressure, diabetes, or structural heart disease
Patients with unmanaged obstructive sleep apnea or thyroid disease
Heavy regular alcohol drinkers and competitive endurance athletes
howToReduceRisk: Screen regularly with a pulse check or smartwatch ECG for irregular pulse rhythm
Manage blood pressure rigorously to prevent left atrial chamber dilation
Treat obstructive sleep apnea with CPAP therapy to reduce nocturnal atrial triggers
Adhere to prescribed oral anticoagulation (DOACs) to prevent cardioembolic stroke
whenToSeeDoctor: An irregular, rapid, or fluttering pulse accompanied by chest pain or dizziness
Signs of stroke: sudden facial droop, arm weakness, or slurred speech (FAST)
Syncope (fainting) or near-blackout episodes during everyday activities
Resting heart rate continuously exceeding 110 beats per minute
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects approximately 33.5 million individuals globally; increases the risk of stroke five-fold if untreated.
reliableSources: AHA / ACC / HRS Guideline for the Management of Atrial Fibrillation
European Heart Rhythm Association (EHRA)
CDC Atrial Fibrillation Resources

diseases.name: Stroke
diseases.shortDescription: A brain emergency occurring when blood flow to an area of the brain is cut off by a clot or a ruptured blood vessel.
diseases.whatIsIt: A stroke is a rapid loss of brain function due to a disturbance in the cerebral blood supply. Ischemic strokes (87% of cases) occur when a blood clot blocks a cerebral artery; hemorrhagic strokes occur when a weakened blood vessel ruptures and bleeds into brain parenchyma.
whyDoesItHappen: Atherosclerotic plaque thrombosis in carotid or intracranial cerebral arteries
Cardioembolic clots traveling from the heart (frequently due to atrial fibrillation)
Severe uncontrolled hypertension rupturing small intracranial perforating vessels
Cerebral aneurysms or arteriovenous malformations (AVMs)
Hypercoagulable states, thrombophilia, or severe carotid artery stenosis
signsYouMayNotice: F - Face Drooping: One side of the face is numb or droops when smiling
A - Arm Weakness: One arm drifts downward or feels paralyzed when raised
S - Speech Difficulty: Slurred words, inability to speak, or difficulty comprehending speech
T - Time to call emergency: Sudden loss of vision in one eye or double vision
Sudden, severe thunderclap headache with no known cause
Loss of balance, vertigo, ataxia, or sudden unexplained clumsiness
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable acute vascular neurological injury. Brain tissue loses approximately 1.9 million neurons every minute during acute ischemia.
whoIsAtRisk: People with hypertension, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, or carotid stenosis
Smokers and individuals with elevated apolipoprotein B / LDL cholesterol
History of prior transient ischemic attack (TIA / mini-stroke)
howToReduceRisk: Target strict systolic blood pressure control below 130 mmHg
Take prescribed anticoagulants if diagnosed with atrial fibrillation
Follow antiplatelet (aspirin / clopidogrel) and high-intensity statin therapy
Eliminate smoking, avoid illicit stimulants, and exercise regularly
whenToSeeDoctor: EMERGENCY: Immediate emergency medical dispatch (911 / 108) at the first sign of FAST symptoms
Even if neurological symptoms resolve within minutes (indicating a TIA requiring urgent evaluation)
Sudden onset of profound dizziness with difficulty walking or swallowing
diseases.howCommonIsIt: The second leading cause of death globally. Over 12 million new strokes occur each year worldwide according to the World Stroke Organization.
reliableSources: American Stroke Association (ASA) / AHA Stroke Guidelines
World Stroke Organization (WSO) Global Stroke Fact Sheet
CDC Stroke Surveillance

diseases.name: Deep Vein Thrombosis & Pulmonary Embolism
diseases.shortDescription: Blood clots forming in deep veins (usually in the legs) that can break free and travel to the lungs, blocking pulmonary blood flow.
diseases.whatIsIt: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) occurs when a thrombus forms in a major deep vein of the lower limb or pelvis. If a fragment of the clot dislodges, it travels through the venous circulation into the pulmonary arterial bed, causing a potentially fatal Pulmonary Embolism (PE).
whyDoesItHappen: Virchow’s triad: venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability
Prolonged immobility during long-haul flights (>4 hours) or bed rest after surgery
Major orthopedic surgeries (total hip or knee replacement) or major pelvic trauma
Malignancy releasing procoagulant factors into the bloodstream
Use of estrogen-containing oral contraceptives or hormone replacement therapy
signsYouMayNotice: Unilateral leg swelling, tightness, or marked asymmetry in calf circumference
Deep, throbbing calf or thigh pain that worsens when walking or flexing the foot
Erythema (redness) and palpable warmth over the affected lower limb vein
Sudden onset of unexplained dyspnea (shortness of breath) and tachypnea
Sharp, pleuritic chest pain that intensifies with deep inspiration or coughing
Coughing up blood (hemoptysis) and rapid heart rate (tachycardia)
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable vascular hematological disorder driven by clotting cascade dysregulation and mechanical venous stasis.
whoIsAtRisk: Patients undergoing orthopedic, cancer, or abdominal surgical procedures
Individuals with hereditary thrombophilias (Factor V Leiden, Prothrombin G20210A)
Cancer patients, pregnant women, and postpartum mothers up to 6 weeks
Hospitalized bedbound patients without pharmacological thromboprophylaxis
howToReduceRisk: Stand up, stretch, and walk down the aisle every 1 to 2 hours during long-distance travel
Wear graduated compression stockings during extended flights or post-operatively
Stay well-hydrated and avoid tight clothing that constricts pelvic venous flow
Take prescribed prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin or DOACs after major surgery
whenToSeeDoctor: EMERGENCY: Sudden shortness of breath, sharp chest pain with breathing, or coughing up blood
Unilateral swelling, persistent redness, and warm tenderness in one calf or thigh
Sudden lightheadedness, cold sweat, or cyanosis (blue discoloration of lips/fingers)
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects an estimated 10 million people worldwide every year; PE is a leading cause of preventable hospital death.
reliableSources: American Society of Hematology (ASH) VTE Guidelines
Chest / ACCP Antithrombotic Therapy for VTE Disease
CDC Venous Thromboembolism Guidance

diseases.name: Peripheral Artery Disease
diseases.shortDescription: A circulatory problem where narrowed arteries reduce blood flow to your limbs, commonly causing leg pain when walking.
diseases.whatIsIt: Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD) is a manifestation of systemic atherosclerosis where fatty deposits obstruct arteries supplying the extremities, primarily the legs. Insufficient arterial perfusion results in intermittent claudication and, in advanced stages, non-healing ischemic ulcers and gangrene.
whyDoesItHappen: Atherosclerotic plaque accumulation within femoral, popliteal, and tibial arteries
Heavy tobacco use promoting arterial endothelial damage and vasoconstriction
Chronic hyperglycemia in diabetes causing micro- and macro-vascular stiffening
Hypertension and elevated circulating LDL cholesterol particles
signsYouMayNotice: Painful cramping in hip, thigh, or calf muscles after walking or climbing stairs (claudication)
Relief of leg cramping after a few minutes of rest
Leg numbness, coldness in lower leg or foot compared to the other side
Sores or ulcers on toes, feet, or legs that heal very slowly or fail to heal
Change in color of legs (pallor when elevated, rubor when dependent)
Hair loss or slower hair growth on feet and legs, and brittle, slow-growing toenails
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable progressive vascular disease; reflects widespread systemic atherosclerosis.
whoIsAtRisk: Smokers (smoking increases PAD risk up to 4-fold)
People with diabetes, hypertension, or hypercholesterolemia over age 50
Individuals with known coronary artery disease or history of stroke
howToReduceRisk: Enroll in a supervised exercise therapy (SET) walking program to develop collateral circulation
Complete smoking cessation (the single most impactful intervention to halt progression)
Take statins and antiplatelet medications to lower the risk of heart attack and limb loss
Inspect feet daily for cuts, blisters, and sores to prevent secondary infection
whenToSeeDoctor: Pain in feet or toes while resting or sleeping (rest pain, a sign of critical limb ischemia)
Non-healing sores, dark discoloration, or black necrotic tissue on toes or feet
A leg or foot that feels markedly colder than the other or becomes suddenly pale
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects over 230 million people worldwide; widely underdiagnosed until advanced ischemic stages.
reliableSources: ACC / AHA Guideline on the Management of Patients With Lower Extremity PAD
Society for Vascular Surgery (SVS) Guidelines
NHLBI Peripheral Artery Disease

diseases.name: Type 1 Diabetes
diseases.medicalName: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1D / Autoimmune Beta-Cell Destruction)
diseases.shortDescription: A chronic autoimmune condition where the pancreas produces little or no insulin, requiring lifelong insulin therapy.
diseases.whatIsIt: In Type 1 Diabetes, the body’s own immune system mistakenly targets and destroys the insulin-producing beta cells in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. Without insulin, glucose cannot enter cells to be used for energy, leading to life-threatening hyperglycemia and diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).
whyDoesItHappen: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells mediated by T-lymphocytes
Genetic susceptibility involving specific HLA-DR and HLA-DQ gene variants
Environmental triggers such as enteroviral infections interacting with genetic traits
Circulating autoantibodies against islet cells (GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8, insulin)
signsYouMayNotice: Excessive, unquenchable thirst (polydipsia) and frequent urination (polyuria)
Rapid, unexplained weight loss despite normal or increased hunger (polyphagia)
Extreme tiredness, lethargy, and lack of physical stamina
Blurred vision due to hyperosmolar changes in the eye lens
Fruity, acetone-smelling breath (a warning sign of impending diabetic ketoacidosis)
Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain accompanied by deep, rapid breathing (Kussmaul breathing)
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable autoimmune disorder; cannot be contracted through contact, diet, or lifestyle factors.
whoIsAtRisk: Children, adolescents, and young adults (though it can develop at any age)
Individuals with a first-degree relative with Type 1 Diabetes
People with other autoimmune disorders (celiac disease, Hashimoto thyroiditis, vitiligo)
howToReduceRisk: Currently no proven prevention method; early diagnosis prevents life-threatening DKA
Monitor blood glucose through continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) systems
Maintain tight time-in-range (70–180 mg/dL > 70% of the day) using multiple daily injections or an insulin pump
Carry fast-acting carbohydrates (glucose tablets, juice) at all times for hypoglycemia management
whenToSeeDoctor: EMERGENCY: Nausea, persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, fruity breath, and high blood sugar (>250 mg/dL)
Severe hypoglycemia (<54 mg/dL) unresponsive to oral glucose or with loss of consciousness (requires glucagon)
New onset of bedwetting in previously toilet-trained children paired with constant thirst
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects approximately 9 million individuals globally, with roughly 1.5 million new pediatric and adult cases diagnosed each year.
reliableSources: American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026
International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes (ISPAD)
JDRF International Type 1 Diabetes Research

diseases.name: PCOS (Polycystic Ovary Syndrome)
diseases.shortDescription: A widespread hormonal imbalance affecting women of reproductive age, leading to irregular periods, elevated androgens, and metabolic challenges.
diseases.whatIsIt: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is a multifaceted endocrine and metabolic disorder diagnosed by the Rotterdam Criteria (at least 2 of 3: irregular ovulation/amenorrhea, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound). It is strongly linked to systemic insulin resistance.
whyDoesItHappen: Hyperinsulinemia stimulating ovarian theca cells to produce excessive androgens (testosterone)
Altered pulsatile gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) leading to elevated LH-to-FSH ratio
Chronic low-grade systemic inflammation stimulating androgen production
Genetic predisposition influencing follicular maturation and insulin signaling pathways
signsYouMayNotice: Infrequent, irregular, or entirely absent menstrual cycles (oligomenorrhea / amenorrhea)
Excess facial and body hair growth (hirsutism) on chin, chest, and abdomen
Severe, cystic acne that resists standard topical skin treatments
Male-pattern hair thinning or scalp hair loss (androgenic alopecia)
Darkened, velvety patches of skin around the neck, groin, and armpits (acanthosis nigricans)
Difficulty conceiving due to infrequent or absent ovulation (anovulatory infertility)
Unexplained weight gain and marked difficulty losing weight around the abdomen
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable complex endocrine and metabolic condition with polygenic and epigenetic origins.
whoIsAtRisk: Women of reproductive age (15 to 45 years)
Family history of PCOS or early-onset Type 2 Diabetes
Women with obesity or significant insulin resistance
howToReduceRisk: Follow a low-glycemic, anti-inflammatory dietary pattern with complex fiber and lean proteins
Aim for 150 minutes of weekly aerobic exercise combined with progressive resistance training
Target a modest 5% to 10% weight reduction, which can restore regular ovulatory cycles
Take prescribed insulin sensitizers (metformin) and cycle-regulating therapies under physician guidance
whenToSeeDoctor: Cycles spaced more than 35 days apart or fewer than 8 periods in a year
Rapidly worsening facial hair growth, deep voice, or significant alopecia
Inability to conceive after 12 months of unprotected regular intercourse (6 months if >35)
Abnormally heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding requiring hourly pad changes
diseases.howCommonIsIt: One of the most common female endocrine disorders, affecting between 8% and 13% of reproductive-age women globally.
reliableSources: International Evidence-Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of PCOS
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG)
Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guidelines

diseases.name: Obesity & Metabolic Syndrome
diseases.shortDescription: A cluster of conditions occurring together that increase your risk of heart disease, stroke, and type 2 diabetes.
diseases.whatIsIt: Metabolic syndrome is defined by having at least 3 of the following 5 risk factors: abdominal visceral obesity (waist circumference >40 inches in men, >35 inches in women), elevated serum triglycerides (>=150 mg/dL), low HDL cholesterol (<40 mg/dL in men, <50 mg/dL in women), elevated blood pressure (>=130/85 mmHg), and elevated fasting blood glucose (>=100 mg/dL).
whyDoesItHappen: Adipocyte hypertrophy and visceral fat accumulation releasing inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-6)
Peripheral insulin resistance in skeletal muscle, hepatic, and adipose tissue
Chronic sedentary behavior and chronic excess caloric intake of refined sugars and trans fats
Disruption of circadian rhythms, chronic sleep deprivation, and high cortisol levels
signsYouMayNotice: Enlarged waistline or protruding visceral abdominal profile
Acanthosis nigricans: darkened, thickened skin folds around neck, knuckles, and axillae
Persistent mid-afternoon energy crashes and craving for high-carbohydrate foods
High resting blood pressure readings during routine screenings
Mild shortness of breath and joint discomfort during physical exertion
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable complex lifestyle and metabolic cluster influenced by genetic, dietary, and environmental factors.
whoIsAtRisk: Adults with sedentary desk jobs and minimal daily physical activity
Individuals with a body mass index (BMI) >= 25 kg/m2 (>= 23 in Asian populations)
People with a family history of diabetes, hypertension, or premature cardiovascular disease
howToReduceRisk: Target a sustainable 7% to 10% reduction in total body weight
Replace ultra-processed snacks and refined grains with legumes, vegetables, and unsaturated fats
Engage in brisk walking for 30 minutes daily and 2 sessions of strength training weekly
Prioritize 7 to 8 hours of restorative sleep to regulate hunger hormones (leptin and ghrelin)
whenToSeeDoctor: Fasting blood glucose consistently reading above 100 mg/dL or HbA1c in prediabetic range (5.7–6.4%)
Blood pressure consistently measuring 130/85 mmHg or higher at home
Fasting lipid panel showing high triglycerides and depressed HDL levels
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects an estimated 25% of the adult world population, representing a major public health challenge.
reliableSources: AHA / NHLBI Scientific Statement on Diagnosis and Management of Metabolic Syndrome
International Diabetes Federation (IDF) Consensus Definition
WHO Obesity and Overweight Factsheet

diseases.name: Osteoporosis
diseases.shortDescription: A silent bone disease that causes bones to become weak and brittle, making them susceptible to fractures from minor falls.
diseases.whatIsIt: Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal condition characterized by low bone mineral density (BMD) and microarchitectural deterioration of bone tissue. Because bone loss happens silently without pain, it is often undiagnosed until a minimal-trauma fragility fracture occurs in the hip, spine, or wrist.
whyDoesItHappen: Imbalance between osteoclast bone resorption and osteoblast bone formation
Postmenopausal estrogen decline accelerating trabecular bone loss in women
Age-related decline in intestinal calcium absorption and cutaneous vitamin D synthesis
Long-term use of systemic glucocorticoid medications (prednisone >5 mg for >3 months)
Chronic medical conditions including hyperthyroidism, celiac disease, and rheumatoid arthritis
signsYouMayNotice: Often no symptoms until a fracture occurs ("the silent disease")
Gradual loss of height over time (1.5 inches or more)
Stooped or hunched forward posture (dorsal kyphosis or "dowager’s hump")
Sudden, severe back pain caused by a collapsed or fractured vertebra
A bone that breaks much more easily than expected (e.g. from a cough or minor bump)
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable progressive degenerative skeletal disorder.
whoIsAtRisk: Postmenopausal women over age 50 and men over age 70
Individuals with small, thin body frames (BMI < 19 kg/m2)
History of maternal or paternal hip fracture
Smokers, heavy alcohol consumers, and individuals with sedentary lifestyles
howToReduceRisk: Obtain 1,200 mg of calcium daily from food and fortified sources combined
Maintain serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels between 30 and 50 ng/mL with supplements as needed
Participate in regular weight-bearing exercises (walking, hiking, stair climbing) and balance training
Undergo routine Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DEXA) bone density screening starting at age 65 (or earlier with risk factors)
Take bone-strengthening medications (bisphosphonates, denosumab) if diagnosed with osteoporosis
whenToSeeDoctor: Any bone fracture occurring after age 50 following a fall from standing height
Unexplained sudden onset of sharp thoracic or lumbar back pain
Noticeable decrease in height of more than 1.5 inches measured over clinical visits
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Causes over 8.9 million fractures annually worldwide; 1 in 3 women and 1 in 5 men over 50 will sustain an osteoporotic fracture.
reliableSources: National Osteoporosis Foundation (NOF) / Bone Health & Osteoporosis Foundation (BHOF)
International Osteoporosis Foundation (IOF) Facts and Statistics
Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guidelines on Osteoporosis

diseases.name: Gout
diseases.medicalName: Acute & Chronic Gouty Arthritis (Monosodium Urate Crystal Arthropathy)
diseases.shortDescription: An intensely painful form of inflammatory arthritis caused by the crystallization of uric acid in joint spaces.
diseases.whatIsIt: Gout is an exquisitely painful inflammatory arthritis caused by hyperuricemia (elevated serum urate >6.8 mg/dL). When serum saturation is exceeded, needle-shaped monosodium urate (MSU) crystals precipitate in synovial fluid and surrounding periarticular tissues, triggering severe localized inflammatory flares (podagra).
whyDoesItHappen: Impaired renal clearance of uric acid (responsible for 90% of hyperuricemia cases)
Overproduction of uric acid due to high intake of purine-rich foods (red meats, organ meats, shellfish)
High consumption of fructose-sweetened sodas and alcohol (especially beer and spirits)
Medications that impair urate excretion (thiazide and loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin)
Comorbidities including hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and metabolic syndrome
signsYouMayNotice: Sudden, excruciating joint pain that often strikes abruptly in the middle of the night
Most commonly affects the base of the big toe (first metatarsophalangeal joint / podagra)
Affected joint becomes hot to the touch, swollen, tense, and intensely red or purplish
Extreme tenderness: even the weight of a light bedsheet on the joint is unbearable
Peeling, itchy skin around the joint as acute inflammation subsides
Development of hard, nodular subcutaneous crystal deposits (tophi) on fingers, elbows, or ears in chronic gout
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable metabolic and inflammatory crystal arthropathy.
whoIsAtRisk: Men aged 30 to 50 (men are 3 times more likely to develop gout than premenopausal women)
Postmenopausal women as protective uricosuric estrogen levels decline
Patients taking long-term loop or thiazide diuretics for hypertension
Individuals with obesity, high alcohol consumption, or renal impairment
howToReduceRisk: Maintain serum uric acid below 6.0 mg/dL (or below 5.0 mg/dL if tophi are present)
Drink plenty of water (2 to 3 liters daily) to promote renal urate clearance
Limit intake of red meat, shellfish, high-fructose corn syrup, and alcoholic beverages
Take prescribed urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol or febuxostat) consistently without stopping during flares
whenToSeeDoctor: Severe, sudden joint pain, swelling, and redness that peaks within 12 to 24 hours
Joint inflammation accompanied by fever and chills (requires joint aspiration to exclude septic arthritis)
Recurrent flares affecting knees, ankles, wrists, or multiple joints
Formation of visible whitish-yellow tophaceous deposits under the skin
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects an estimated 41 million people globally; the most common form of inflammatory arthritis in adult men.
reliableSources: American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Guideline for the Management of Gout
European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) Gout Recommendations
CDC Gout Overview

diseases.name: Migraine
diseases.shortDescription: A severe, recurring neurological headache disorder characterized by throbbing pain, sensory hypersensitivity, and nausea.
diseases.whatIsIt: Migraine is not just a bad headache; it is a complex genetic neurovascular disorder involving cortical spreading depression and activation of the trigeminovascular sensory system, leading to sterile neurogenic inflammation around cerebral and dural blood vessels.
whyDoesItHappen: Sensitization and activation of the trigeminovascular nerve pathway
Release of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and substance P promoting vasodilation and neuroinflammation
Cortical spreading depression: a wave of depolarizing neuronal and glial activity across the cerebral cortex causing aura
Genetic susceptibility involving ion channel genes and neurotransmitter receptors
Hormonal fluctuations (especially estrogen drops prior to menstruation)
Environmental and sensory triggers: bright flickering lights, loud sounds, strong odors, skipped meals, and sleep disruption
signsYouMayNotice: Unilateral (one-sided) throbbing or pulsating moderate-to-severe head pain
Headache aggravated by routine physical activity like walking or climbing stairs
Intense sensitivity to light (photophobia) and sensitivity to sound (phonophobia)
Nausea, queasiness, and sometimes vomiting
Visual aura: zigzagging lines, shimmering lights, blind spots (scotoma) preceding headache by 20 to 60 minutes
Postdrome "migraine hangover": lingering exhaustion, brain fog, and neck stiffness for 24 hours after pain subsides
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable complex primary neurobiological headache disorder with polygenic inheritance.
whoIsAtRisk: Women (three times more common in women due to hormonal influences)
Individuals aged 18 to 44 years
People with a family history of migraine (70% of sufferers have a first-degree relative)
howToReduceRisk: Maintain a consistent daily sleep schedule, waking up and going to bed at the same time
Avoid skipping meals and stay well-hydrated throughout the day
Keep a migraine diary to identify and avoid individual dietary and environmental triggers
Discuss preventive therapies (CGRP inhibitors, beta-blockers, topiramate) with a neurologist if headaches occur >= 4 days/month
whenToSeeDoctor: Sudden onset of an explosive "thunderclap" headache reaching maximal intensity in seconds
Headache accompanied by fever, stiff neck, confusion, seizure, or double vision
New headache starting after age 50 or in a person with a history of cancer
Headache that worsens progressively over days or weeks or changes pattern abruptly
diseases.howCommonIsIt: The second leading cause of disability worldwide, affecting over 1 billion people across the globe.
reliableSources: American Headache Society (AHS) Consensus Statement
International Headache Society (IHS) - ICHD-3 Classification
WHO Headache Disorders Factsheet

diseases.name: Epilepsy
diseases.medicalName: Epilepsy & Recurrent Seizure Disorders (Paroxysmal Cerebral Dysrhythmia)
diseases.shortDescription: A chronic neurological condition characterized by recurrent, unprovoked seizures caused by abnormal electrical brain activity.
diseases.whatIsIt: Epilepsy is defined by having two or more unprovoked seizures occurring more than 24 hours apart, or one unprovoked seizure with a high probability of recurrence. During a seizure, clusters of neurons in the brain fire in an abnormal, excessive, and hypersynchronous electrical pattern.
whyDoesItHappen: Genetic mutations affecting neuronal voltage-gated ion channels or neurotransmitter receptors
Structural brain damage from head trauma, stroke, or lack of oxygen during birth
Central nervous system infections (meningitis, encephalitis, neurocysticercosis)
Brain tumors or congenital cerebral cortical dysplasias (developmental anomalies)
Underlying metabolic imbalances or neurodegenerative disorders
signsYouMayNotice: Focal seizures: involuntary jerking of an arm or leg, sensory tingling, unusual tastes or smells, or sudden déja vu
Generalized tonic-clonic seizures: sudden loss of consciousness, body stiffening (tonic phase) followed by rhythmic jerking (clonic phase)
Absence seizures: brief staring spells lasting 5 to 15 seconds with no memory of the event
Tongue biting (especially lateral border), loss of bladder control, and deep labored breathing during a seizure
Post-ictal state: confusion, deep drowsiness, headache, and sore muscles for 15 to 60 minutes after consciousness returns
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable neurological disease; cannot be transmitted between people.
whoIsAtRisk: Young children and older adults over age 65 (highest incidence)
Individuals with a history of traumatic brain injury (TBI) or stroke
Children who experienced prolonged febrile seizures in infancy
howToReduceRisk: Take prescribed anti-seizure medications (AEDs) consistently without missing doses
Maintain regular sleep hygiene; avoid sleep deprivation (a major seizure trigger)
Wear helmets during contact sports and cycling to prevent traumatic brain injuries
Limit alcohol consumption and avoid recreational drugs and flashing strobe lights if photosensitive
whenToSeeDoctor: EMERGENCY: Call emergency services if a seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes (status epilepticus)
EMERGENCY: Call if a second seizure begins immediately without regaining consciousness between them
First-time seizure in an individual who has never had a seizure before
Seizure occurring in water or resulting in a head injury or difficulty breathing
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects roughly 50 million people worldwide; approximately 70% of people with epilepsy can live seizure-free with proper medication.
reliableSources: International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) Guidelines
American Epilepsy Society (AES)
World Health Organization (WHO) Epilepsy Factsheet

diseases.name: Alzheimer’s Disease & Dementia
diseases.shortDescription: A progressive neurodegenerative brain disease that slowly destroys memory, thinking skills, and the ability to carry out everyday tasks.
diseases.whatIsIt: Alzheimer’s disease is the most common form of dementia (accounting for 60% to 70% of cases). It is characterized pathologically by the accumulation of extracellular beta-amyloid plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau protein, resulting in progressive synaptic loss and cerebral cortical atrophy.
whyDoesItHappen: Abnormal cleavage and aggregation of amyloid precursor protein (APP) forming amyloid-beta plaques
Hyperphosphorylation of tau protein causing microtubule collapse and neurofibrillary tangles
Genetic risk factors, notably the Apolipoprotein E epsilon-4 (APOE-e4) allele
Cerebral microvascular dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and impaired glymphatic clearance
Advancing age (the single greatest known risk factor)
signsYouMayNotice: Memory loss that disrupts daily life: forgetting recently learned information and important dates
Challenges in planning, problem-solving, or tracking monthly finances and recipes
Difficulty completing familiar tasks at home, work, or leisure
Confusion with time or place: losing track of dates, seasons, or where one is
Trouble understanding visual images and spatial relationships
New problems with words in speaking or writing (struggling to name familiar objects)
Misplacing things and losing the ability to retrace steps to find them
Changes in mood, personality, and social withdrawal (unwarranted suspicion, apathy)
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable progressive neurodegenerative disease.
whoIsAtRisk: Individuals aged 65 and older (risk doubles every 5 years past age 65)
Individuals with a family history or carrying the APOE-e4 gene variant
People with untreated cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, midlife obesity)
Individuals with history of traumatic brain injury or low cognitive/social engagement
howToReduceRisk: Engage in lifelong intellectual, mental, and social stimulation
Adopt a MIND or Mediterranean diet rich in berries, leafy greens, nuts, and fish
Maintain rigorous blood pressure and cardiovascular risk control throughout midlife
Ensure 7 to 8 hours of restorative sleep to support glymphatic clearance of brain amyloid
Promptly treat hearing loss with hearing aids to reduce cognitive isolation
whenToSeeDoctor: Noticeable, progressive memory impairment or confusion noticed by family members
Getting lost while driving or walking in familiar neighborhoods
Difficulty managing prescribed medications, personal hygiene, or financial obligations
Uncharacteristic aggressive behavior, paranoia, or severe wandering
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Over 55 million people worldwide currently live with dementia; projected to reach 139 million by 2050.
reliableSources: Alzheimer’s Association Facts and Figures 2026
National Institute on Aging (NIA) / NIH Alzheimer’s Information
World Health Organization (WHO) Global Action Plan on Dementia

diseases.name: Parkinson’s Disease
diseases.shortDescription: A progressive nervous system disorder that affects movement, causing tremors, stiffness, and balance difficulties.
diseases.whatIsIt: Parkinson’s disease is a neurodegenerative movement disorder marked by the progressive loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta of the brainstem, accompanied by the intracellular accumulation of misfolded alpha-synuclein proteins (Lewy bodies).
whyDoesItHappen: Selective death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra reducing basal ganglia motor control
Aggregation of misfolded alpha-synuclein protein into cytotoxic Lewy bodies
Mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and impaired autophagy in neuronal cells
Complex interaction between genetic mutations (SNCA, LRRK2, PRKN, GBA) and environmental toxins (pesticides, heavy metals)
signsYouMayNotice: Resting tremor: rhythmic shaking that typically begins in one hand or fingers ("pill-rolling" tremor)
Bradykinesia: slowness of voluntary movement, making everyday actions take significantly longer
Muscle rigidity: stiffness in limbs and neck that resists passive movement ("cogwheel rigidity")
Postural instability and impaired balance: stooped posture, reduced arm swing when walking, and shuffling gait with short steps
Hypomimia (masked facial expression) and soft, monotone voice (hypophonia)
Micrographia: handwriting that becomes abnormally small and cramped
Non-motor symptoms: loss of smell (anosmia), REM sleep behavior disorder, and chronic constipation often preceding motor signs by years
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable neurodegenerative disorder.
whoIsAtRisk: Adults over age 60 (incidence increases steeply with age)
Men are approximately 1.5 times more likely to develop Parkinson’s than women
Individuals with chronic occupational exposure to agricultural pesticides and herbicides
Family members of individuals with early-onset Parkinson’s disease
howToReduceRisk: Engage in regular, vigorous aerobic exercise (cycling, boxing, dance) which demonstrates neuroprotective benefits
Moderate caffeine consumption (coffee/tea) has been correlated with reduced risk in observational cohorts
Avoid unshielded occupational exposure to pesticides, solvents, and herbicides
whenToSeeDoctor: Persistent involuntary resting tremor in one hand, thumb, or chin
Noticeable slowing of everyday movements (trouble buttoning shirts, getting up from chairs)
Balance difficulties, unsteadiness, or frequent unprovoked falls
Stiffness or rigidity in limbs accompanied by a soft, monotone voice
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects over 10 million people worldwide; it is the fastest-growing neurological disorder in prevalence and disability.
reliableSources: Movement Disorder Society (MDS) Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Parkinson’s Disease
Parkinson’s Foundation / Michael J. Fox Foundation
National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS)

diseases.name: Multiple Sclerosis
diseases.shortDescription: A chronic autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks the protective myelin sheath covering nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord.
diseases.whatIsIt: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is an immune-mediated inflammatory demyelinating condition of the central nervous system. When the myelin sheath and underlying axons are damaged, nerve impulses are slowed or blocked, resulting in diverse motor, sensory, visual, and cognitive deficits.
whyDoesItHappen: Auto-reactive T-cells and B-cells crossing the blood-brain barrier and attacking myelin basic protein
Oligodendrocyte cell loss leading to localized demyelinated plaques (scleroses) in white and gray matter
Genetic susceptibility involving HLA-DRB1*15:01 allele
Environmental risk factors: low sun exposure / Vitamin D deficiency, cigarette smoking, childhood obesity, and prior Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) infection
signsYouMayNotice: Optic neuritis: sudden painful vision loss or blurring, typically in one eye, with washed-out color vision
Paresthesias: numbness, tingling, or electric-shock sensations that radiate down the spine when bending the neck (Lhermitte’s sign)
Limb weakness, muscle spasticity, and difficulty walking with unsteady gait
Profound, overwhelming fatigue that worsens significantly in hot weather or warm showers (Uhthoff’s phenomenon)
Bladder dysfunction: urinary urgency, incontinence, or incomplete emptying
Vertigo, double vision (diplopia), and cognitive changes in memory and processing speed
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable autoimmune demyelinating disease.
whoIsAtRisk: Young adults between 20 and 40 years of age
Women (nearly 3 times more frequently diagnosed than men)
Populations residing in higher latitudes further from the equator (temperate zones)
Individuals with a personal or family history of autoimmune diseases
howToReduceRisk: Maintain adequate Vitamin D levels through sensible sun exposure and supplementation
Do not smoke cigarettes; smoking accelerates the transition to progressive disability
Initiate high-efficacy Disease-Modifying Therapies (DMTs) early after diagnosis to prevent permanent axonal loss
whenToSeeDoctor: Sudden loss of vision or eye pain during eye movement lasting several days
Persistent numbness or weakness in one side of the body lasting more than 24 hours
Sudden loss of balance, double vision, or inability to control bladder function
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects approximately 2.9 million people worldwide; modern DMTs have revolutionized long-term disease outcomes.
reliableSources: National Multiple Sclerosis Society (NMSS) Clinical Guidelines
McDonald Diagnostic Criteria for Multiple Sclerosis (2024 Revisions)
Multiple Sclerosis International Federation (MSIF)

diseases.name: Meningitis
diseases.medicalName: Acute Meningitis (Bacterial / Viral / Fungal Leptomeningeal Infection)
diseases.shortDescription: A serious and potentially life-threatening inflammation of the protective membranes (meninges) surrounding the brain and spinal cord.
diseases.whatIsIt: Meningitis is an acute infection of the subarachnoid space and leptomeninges. Bacterial meningitis (caused by Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, or Haemophilus influenzae) is a medical emergency that can cause death or brain damage within hours if untreated with antibiotics.
whyDoesItHappen: Bacterial colonization of the nasopharynx followed by bacteremia and crossing the blood-brain barrier
Viral infections (enteroviruses, herpes simplex virus, arboviruses)
Direct spread from adjacent severe infections (otitis media, mastoiditis, sinusitis) or cranial trauma
Fungal pathogens (Cryptococcus neoformans) in immunocompromised patients (HIV/AIDS)
signsYouMayNotice: Classic Triad: sudden high fever, severe unremitting headache, and pronounced neck stiffness (nuchal rigidity)
Inability to flex chin to chest without severe discomfort or involuntary knee flexion (Brudzinski’s sign)
Severe photophobia (pain when looking at bright light) and phonophobia
Altered mental status: confusion, lethargy, delirium, or difficulty waking up
Non-blanching purpuric or petechial rash (hallmark of Neisseria meningitidis meningococcemia)
In infants: high-pitched cry, bulging fontanelle, irritability, and refusal to feed
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Bacterial and viral strains spread through respiratory droplets and saliva from coughing, sneezing, kissing, or sharing drinks.
whoIsAtRisk: Infants, young children, and college students living in crowded dormitories
Individuals with anatomic or functional asplenia (missing spleen)
People with complement component deficiencies or HIV/AIDS
howToReduceRisk: Receive all recommended vaccines: Meningococcal (MenACWY and MenB), Pneumococcal (PCV/PPSV), and Hib
Do not share drinking glasses, water bottles, eating utensils, or lip balm
Provide post-exposure antibiotic chemoprophylaxis (rifampin, ciprofloxacin) to close contacts of confirmed bacterial cases
whenToSeeDoctor: EMERGENCY: Immediate emergency hospitalization for high fever, stiff neck, and confusion
Any dark purple or red pinprick rash that does not fade when a clear glass is pressed against it
Seizures or lethargy occurring in a patient with a severe headache
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Bacterial meningitis affects an estimated 1.2 million people annually worldwide, carrying a high case fatality rate of 10% to 20% even with treatment.
reliableSources: World Health Organization (WHO) Defeating Meningitis by 2030 Roadmap
CDC Meningococcal Disease Surveillance
Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) Meningitis Guidelines

diseases.name: Pneumonia
diseases.shortDescription: An infection that inflames the air sacs in one or both lungs, which may fill with fluid or purulent material.
diseases.whatIsIt: Pneumonia is an acute lower respiratory tract infection in which the pulmonary alveoli become filled with inflammatory exudate, pus, and cellular debris. This impairs oxygen diffusion into pulmonary capillaries, causing hypoxemia, chest pain, and severe cough.
whyDoesItHappen: Bacterial infection, most frequently Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, or Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Viral pathogens including Influenza A/B, Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), and SARS-CoV-2
Micro-aspiration of colonized oral secretions during sleep or impaired consciousness
Inhalation of aerosolized fungal spores (Histoplasma, Coccidioides) in specific endemic areas
signsYouMayNotice: Persistent cough producing greenish, yellow, or rust-colored sputum
High fever accompanied by shaking chills and profuse drenching sweats
Sharp or stabbing chest pain that worsens when breathing deeply or coughing (pleuritic chest pain)
Shortness of breath, tachypnea (rapid breathing), and decreased oxygen saturation (<94%)
Extreme fatigue, muscle aches, loss of appetite, and headache
In older adults: confusion, delirium, or hypothermia rather than fever
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Spreads through airborne droplets from coughs and sneezes, and through aspiration of oral secretions.
whoIsAtRisk: Adults aged 65 and older and children under 5 years of age
Smokers and individuals with chronic lung diseases (COPD, asthma, bronchiectasis)
Individuals with compromised immune systems (chemotherapy, organ transplant, HIV)
howToReduceRisk: Get vaccinated: Pneumococcal conjugate (PCV20/PCV15), annual Influenza, and COVID-19 vaccines
Practice diligent hand hygiene and dental hygiene to reduce pathogenic oral bacteria
Avoid smoking and second-hand smoke exposure to preserve respiratory mucociliary clearance
whenToSeeDoctor: Difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain, or high fever lasting more than 3 days
Oxygen saturation reading below 92% on a home pulse oximeter
Coughing up blood or dark rust-colored mucus
New onset confusion, lethargy, or blue lips/fingertips (cyanosis)
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects over 450 million people each year globally and remains the leading infectious cause of death in children under 5 and frail elderly adults.
reliableSources: ATS / IDSA Community-Acquired Pneumonia Clinical Guidelines
British Thoracic Society (BTS) Pneumonia Guidelines
CDC Pneumonia Resources

diseases.name: COPD (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease)
diseases.medicalName: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (Emphysema & Chronic Bronchitis)
diseases.shortDescription: A progressive lung disease characterized by long-term breathing difficulties and poor airflow that does not fully reverse.
diseases.whatIsIt: COPD encompasses chronic bronchitis (airway inflammation and hypersecretion of mucus for at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years) and emphysema (destruction of alveolar walls and loss of lung elastic recoil). It causes dynamic air trapping, hyperinflation, and progressive exercise intolerance.
whyDoesItHappen: Long-term tobacco smoking (responsible for over 70% of cases in high-income countries)
Chronic exposure to indoor air pollution from burning biomass fuels (wood, dung) in poorly ventilated stoves
Occupational exposure to industrial chemical fumes, silica, and mineral dusts
Genetic deficiency of Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AATD), leading to uninhibited elastase destruction of lung tissue
signsYouMayNotice: Progressive shortness of breath, especially noticeable during physical exertion ("air hunger")
Chronic, daily cough that produces significant amounts of clear, white, or discolored sputum ("smoker’s cough")
Frequent respiratory infections that take longer than normal to resolve
Wheezing, chest tightness, and the sensation that lungs cannot empty completely
Use of accessory breathing muscles (neck and shoulder lifting during inhalation)
Unintended weight loss and muscle wasting (pulmonary cachexia) in advanced stages
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable progressive inflammatory lung disease caused by inhaled toxic particles and gases.
whoIsAtRisk: Current and former tobacco smokers over age 40
People exposed to long-term biomass smoke, second-hand smoke, or industrial dusts
Individuals with a childhood history of severe asthma or frequent respiratory infections
howToReduceRisk: Complete and permanent smoking cessation (the only intervention that slows FEV1 decline)
Receive annual flu, pneumococcal, RSV, and pertussis vaccinations to prevent acute exacerbations
Participate in pulmonary rehabilitation to improve physical stamina and breathing mechanics
Use prescribed long-acting bronchodilators (LAMA / LABA) and inhaled corticosteroids consistently
whenToSeeDoctor: Sudden increase in shortness of breath and sputum volume or change in sputum color (acute exacerbation)
Resting oxygen saturation dropping below 88% (requires supplemental oxygen assessment)
Blue discoloration of lips or fingernail beds (cyanosis) or confusion/somnolence (carbon dioxide retention)
diseases.howCommonIsIt: The third leading cause of death globally, responsible for over 3.2 million deaths annually according to the WHO.
reliableSources: Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) 2026 Report
American Thoracic Society (ATS) / European Respiratory Society (ERS)
World Health Organization (WHO) COPD Factsheet

diseases.name: Bronchitis
diseases.shortDescription: Inflammation of the lining of your bronchial tubes, which carry air to and from your lungs, causing persistent coughing.
diseases.whatIsIt: Acute bronchitis is an inflammation of the tracheobronchial tree, usually following an upper respiratory viral illness. It is self-limiting and rarely requires antibiotics. In contrast, chronic bronchitis is a progressive subtype of COPD characterized by productive cough lasting at least 3 months per year for 2 consecutive years.
whyDoesItHappen: Viral infections in >90% of acute cases (influenza, parainfluenza, RSV, rhinovirus)
Bacterial superinfection in individuals with underlying airway damage
Inhalation of environmental irritants (cigarette smoke, chemical fumes, severe urban smog)
Chronic tobacco use and industrial dust exposure driving chronic bronchitis
signsYouMayNotice: Persistent, nagging cough that produces clear, yellow, or green mucus
Cough that lingers for 2 to 3 weeks after other cold symptoms have disappeared
Substernal burning or chest soreness worsened by deep coughing fits
Mild fever, low-grade chills, and generalized fatigue
Wheezing or slight shortness of breath when walking briskly
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Acute viral forms spread via respiratory airborne droplets and hand-to-face contact with contaminated surfaces.
whoIsAtRisk: Smokers and individuals living with smokers
People with weakened immune defenses, asthma, or chronic sinus disease
Individuals with frequent exposure to chemical fumes, grain dust, or textile fibers
howToReduceRisk: Avoid tobacco smoke and wear an N95 respirator in dusty or chemical-heavy work environments
Use a cool-mist humidifier at home to moisten airway passages and ease mucus clearance
Get vaccinated annually against influenza, COVID-19, and whooping cough (pertussis)
whenToSeeDoctor: Cough lasting more than 3 weeks without improvement
Fever higher than 100.4°F (38°C) or fever recurring after several days
Coughing up blood or rust-colored phlegm
Difficulty breathing or wheezing that disrupts sleep
diseases.howCommonIsIt: One of the top 10 most common outpatient diagnoses; acute bronchitis accounts for millions of doctor visits every winter.
reliableSources: CDC Acute Bronchitis Clinical Guidance
American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP) Bronchitis Overview
National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)

diseases.name: Sleep Apnea
diseases.medicalName: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA / Upper Airway Nocturnal Collapse)
diseases.shortDescription: A potentially serious sleep disorder in which breathing repeatedly stops and starts during sleep due to throat muscle relaxation.
diseases.whatIsIt: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) is characterized by recurrent episodes of upper airway partial (hypopnea) or complete (apnea) obstruction during sleep. Each collapse causes arterial oxygen desaturation, surges in sympathetic tone, and brief cortical arousals that fragment sleep architecture.
whyDoesItHappen: Excess soft tissue in the pharynx, enlarged tonsils, or thick neck circumference (>17 inches in men, >16 inches in women)
Relaxation of the tongue and soft palate muscles during deep REM sleep blocking the pharyngeal lumen
Craniofacial features such as a retrognathic (receded) lower jaw or narrow hard palate
Alcohol, sedatives, or muscle relaxants prior to bed worsening pharyngeal hypotonia
signsYouMayNotice: Loud, chronic, disruptive snoring punctuated by periods of silence followed by gasping or choking
Witnessed breathing pauses during sleep observed by a bed partner
Waking up with a dry mouth, sore throat, or morning frontal headache
Excessive daytime sleepiness (falling asleep while driving, reading, or watching television)
Difficulty concentrating, memory deficits, mood irritability, and depression
Frequent waking at night to urinate (nocturia) and decreased libido
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable anatomic and neuromuscular sleep breathing disorder.
whoIsAtRisk: Men (twice as common in men as premenopausal women)
Individuals with overweight or obesity (BMI > 30 kg/m2)
People with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, or treatment-resistant atrial fibrillation
howToReduceRisk: Target weight loss; a 10% weight reduction can yield up to a 50% decrease in apnea severity
Avoid alcohol and sedative medications for at least 4 hours before bedtime
Sleep on your side rather than your back using positional therapy devices or pillows
Undergo a formal polysomnography (sleep study) and adhere to continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy
whenToSeeDoctor: Bed partner observes you repeatedly stopping breathing or choking in your sleep
Severe daytime drowsiness causing you to doze off while driving or working
High blood pressure that remains uncontrolled despite taking three different medications
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects nearly 1 billion adults worldwide (over 425 million with moderate-to-severe disease); over 80% remain undiagnosed.
reliableSources: American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) OSA Practice Guidelines
Lancet Respiratory Medicine Global Burden of OSA Study
National Sleep Foundation

diseases.name: COVID-19
diseases.shortDescription: A contagious respiratory illness caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus, ranging from mild symptoms to severe viral pneumonia.
diseases.whatIsIt: COVID-19 is an acute viral disease caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). The virus binds to human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptors found on respiratory epithelial cells, vascular endothelium, and multiple organ systems.
whyDoesItHappen: Infection by SARS-CoV-2 virus variants (Omicron sub-lineages and emerging recombinant clades)
Inhalation of viral aerosol particles emitted during talking, singing, coughing, or heavy breathing
Host immune dysregulation: hyperinflammatory cytokine release causing microvascular thrombosis and alveolar damage in severe cases
signsYouMayNotice: Fever or chills, dry cough, and shortness of breath or difficulty breathing
Sudden loss of taste (ageusia) or smell (anosmia)
Fatigue, muscle or body aches (myalgia), and headache
Sore throat, congestion, runny nose, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea
Long COVID / Post-COVID condition: brain fog, persistent fatigue, post-exertional malaise, and dysautonomia lasting >12 weeks
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Highly contagious through aerosolized respiratory micro-droplets in indoor spaces with inadequate ventilation.
whoIsAtRisk: Adults aged 65 and older
Individuals with underlying conditions (cardiovascular disease, diabetes, obesity, chronic lung or kidney disease)
Unvaccinated individuals and immunocompromised patients
howToReduceRisk: Stay updated with updated annual COVID-19 booster vaccinations
Improve indoor air ventilation (HEPA filters, opening windows) and wear high-filtration masks (N95/KF94) in crowded indoor settings
Use rapid antigen tests when symptoms appear; begin oral antivirals (Paxlovid) within 5 days of onset if high-risk
whenToSeeDoctor: EMERGENCY: Trouble breathing, persistent pain or pressure in the chest, new confusion
Oxygen saturation dropping below 94% on a pulse oximeter
Inability to wake or stay awake, or pale, gray, or blue skin, lips, or nail beds
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Over 775 million confirmed cases globally; continues to circulate endemically worldwide with seasonal waves.
reliableSources: World Health Organization (WHO) COVID-19 Technical Guidance
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) COVID-19 Clinical Management
NIH COVID-19 Treatment Guidelines

diseases.name: GERD (Acid Reflux)
diseases.shortDescription: A digestive disorder that occurs when stomach acid repeatedly flows back up into the tube connecting your mouth and stomach.
diseases.whatIsIt: GERD is a chronic condition in which gastric acid and digestive enzymes flow backward past an incompetent lower esophageal sphincter (LES) into the esophagus, causing mucosal irritation, chemical injury, and potentially Barrett’s esophagus (a precancerous change).
whyDoesItHappen: Transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations (TLESRs) or decreased basal LES resting pressure
Hiatal hernia: the upper part of the stomach pushes upward through the diaphragm hiatus
Delayed gastric emptying and elevated intra-abdominal pressure from obesity or pregnancy
Dietary triggers (fatty/fried foods, chocolate, caffeine, alcohol, peppermint, citrus, tomato sauce)
Lying down immediately after large meals and smoking cigarettes
signsYouMayNotice: Pyrosis (heartburn): a burning sensation in the center of the chest behind the breastbone, usually after eating
Regurgitation: a sour or bitter-tasting acid liquid backing up into the throat or mouth
Dysphagia: difficulty swallowing or the sensation of food feeling stuck in the chest
Chronic dry cough, hoarseness, clearing of the throat, or laryngitis (laryngopharyngeal reflux)
Worsening of asthma symptoms and dental enamel erosion from acid contact
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable gastrointestinal motility and anatomical disorder.
whoIsAtRisk: Individuals with overweight, obesity, or large visceral waist circumferences
Pregnant women due to progesterone-mediated sphincter relaxation
People with hiatal hernias, connective tissue disorders (scleroderma), or gastroparesis
howToReduceRisk: Elevate the head of your bed 6 to 8 inches using bed risers or a wedge pillow (not just extra pillows)
Wait at least 3 hours after eating before lying down or going to sleep
Eat smaller, more frequent meals and avoid identified dietary acid triggers
Take prescribed proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) or H2-receptor antagonists under physician supervision
whenToSeeDoctor: Difficulty or pain when swallowing (dysphagia / odynophagia)
Vomiting blood (hematemesis) or passing black, tarry stools (melena)
Unintended weight loss or persistent choking sensations at night
Heartburn occurring more than twice a week for years (requires screening for Barrett’s esophagus)
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects an estimated 20% of the adult population in North America and Europe, with rising incidence across Asia.
reliableSources: American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) Guidelines for GERD
World Gastroenterology Organisation (WGO) Global Guidelines
American Gastroenterological Association (AGA)

diseases.name: Peptic Ulcer Disease
diseases.medicalName: Peptic Ulcer Disease (Gastric & Duodenal Mucosal Ulceration)
diseases.shortDescription: Painful sores that develop in the lining of the stomach (gastric ulcer) or the first part of your small intestine (duodenal ulcer).
diseases.whatIsIt: Peptic ulcer disease occurs when the protective mucosal barrier of the stomach or duodenum is broken down by the destructive actions of gastric hydrochloric acid and pepsin, eroding through the muscularis mucosae and risking gastrointestinal hemorrhage or perforation.
whyDoesItHappen: Helicobacter pylori bacterial infection of the gastric antrum and corpus (causes >70% of ulcers)
Regular, frequent use of Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs: ibuprofen, naproxen, high-dose aspirin)
Concurrent use of NSAIDs with corticosteroids, anticoagulants, or SSRIs
Heavy tobacco smoking and high alcohol intake impairing mucosal blood flow
Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (rare gastrinoma hypersecreting massive acid)
signsYouMayNotice: Burning epigastric stomach pain that occurs between meals or in the middle of the night
Duodenal ulcer pain typically improves temporarily with food or antacids, then returns 2 to 3 hours later
Gastric ulcer pain often worsens shortly after eating food
Feeling of premature fullness, bloating, belching, and nausea
Intolerance to fatty foods and unexplained loss of appetite
Severe complications: vomiting dark material resembling coffee grounds or passing black tarry stools (melena)
diseases.howDoesItSpread: H. pylori is transmitted from person to person through oral-oral or fecal-oral routes (contaminated food and water).
whoIsAtRisk: People harboring Helicobacter pylori infection
Chronic daily users of NSAIDs for arthritis, back pain, or headaches
Adults over 60 years of age and individuals with prior ulcer history
howToReduceRisk: Test for and eradicate H. pylori with guideline-recommended quadruple antibiotic therapy
Avoid long-term daily NSAID use; co-prescribe a PPI if NSAID therapy is mandatory
Wash hands thoroughly with soap before meals and eat properly cooked, safe foods
whenToSeeDoctor: EMERGENCY: Sudden, severe, sharp "board-like" abdominal pain (sign of gastric perforation)
Vomiting blood or coffee-ground material
Passing black, sticky, tarry stools with a foul odor
Unexplained dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting (severe blood loss)
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects approximately 4 million individuals annually; lifetime prevalence is roughly 5% to 10% in the general population.
reliableSources: American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) Clinical Guideline on Treatment of H. pylori
Maastricht VI / Florence Consensus Report on H. pylori Management
CDC Helicobacter pylori Overview

diseases.name: IBS (Irritable Bowel Syndrome)
diseases.medicalName: Irritable Bowel Syndrome (Disorder of Gut-Brain Interaction / DGBI)
diseases.shortDescription: A common disorder that affects the large intestine, causing abdominal cramping, gas, bloating, and changes in bowel habits.
diseases.whatIsIt: IBS is a functional disorder of gut-brain interaction (DGBI) diagnosed using Rome IV criteria. It is characterized by recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation, accompanied by a change in stool frequency or form, without visible structural mucosal abnormalities.
whyDoesItHappen: Dysregulation of bidirectional communication along the gut-brain axis
Visceral hypersensitivity: lower pain threshold in response to normal bowel distension and gas
Altered gut motility: accelerated transit in IBS-D (diarrhea) or slowed transit in IBS-C (constipation)
Post-infectious low-grade intestinal inflammation following severe food poisoning (Post-Infectious IBS)
Intestinal dysbiosis and increased epithelial permeability ("leaky gut")
signsYouMayNotice: Recurrent abdominal cramping or aching that is often relieved or worsened after a bowel movement
IBS-C: infrequent, hard, lumpy stools requiring excessive straining
IBS-D: frequent, urgent, watery or loose stools, often worst in the morning
IBS-M: alternating periods of both constipation and diarrhea
Persistent abdominal bloating, visible abdominal distension, and excessive gas
Feeling of incomplete bowel evacuation (tenesmus) and whitish mucus in the stool
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable functional gastrointestinal disorder.
whoIsAtRisk: Young adults under age 50 (two times more common in women than men)
Individuals with high chronic stress, anxiety, or depression
People who have had a prior acute episode of severe infectious gastroenteritis
howToReduceRisk: Follow a structured Low-FODMAP elimination and reintroduction diet under a specialized dietitian
Engage in regular physical activity to stimulate natural, rhythmic colonic transit
Practice gut-directed hypnotherapy or cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) to calm gut-brain signaling
Increase soluble fiber (psyllium) while avoiding insoluble fiber (coarse wheat bran) in IBS-C
whenToSeeDoctor: RED FLAGS (not IBS): Rectal bleeding or blood mixed in the stool
Unexplained, involuntary weight loss
Diarrhea that wakes you up from sleep at night (nocturnal diarrhea)
Onset of new bowel habit changes starting after age 50 (requires colonoscopy)
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects an estimated 9% to 15% of the global population, significantly impacting quality of life and productivity.
reliableSources: Rome Foundation - Rome IV Criteria for Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction
American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) Clinical Guideline: Management of IBS
World Gastroenterology Organisation (WGO) IBS Global Guidelines

diseases.name: IBD (Crohn’s & Ulcerative Colitis)
diseases.medicalName: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (Crohn’s Disease & Ulcerative Colitis)
diseases.shortDescription: Chronic autoimmune conditions involving severe, long-term inflammation of the tissues in your digestive tract.
diseases.whatIsIt: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) consists of Crohn’s Disease (transmural, patchy inflammation that can affect any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus) and Ulcerative Colitis (continuous mucosal inflammation restricted to the colon and rectum). Both are chronic relapsing-remitting immune-mediated diseases.
whyDoesItHappen: Inappropriate mucosal immune response to normal gut microbiota in genetically predisposed individuals
Overproduction of inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-12, IL-23, integrins)
Breakdown of intestinal epithelial barrier integrity allowing bacterial antigen translocation
Over 200 genetic loci identified (NOD2, ATG16L1, IL23R)
Environmental factors: Western high-fat diet, frequent antibiotic use in childhood, smoking (worsens Crohn’s)
signsYouMayNotice: Persistent, severe diarrhea often containing visible blood, pus, and mucus
Cramping abdominal pain (frequently right lower quadrant in Crohn’s; left-sided in Colitis)
Urgent need to move bowels (fecal urgency) and painful straining with little stool (tenesmus)
Unexplained weight loss, malnutrition, and growth failure in children
Low-grade fever and fatigue related to chronic systemic inflammation
Extraintestinal manifestations: painful red eye (uveitis), mouth ulcers, joint swelling, and tender skin nodules (erythema nodosum)
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable chronic immune-mediated inflammatory bowel disease.
whoIsAtRisk: Individuals between 15 and 35 years of age (peak onset)
Individuals with a first-degree family member diagnosed with IBD
Populations in industrialized, urbanized environments with Western diets
howToReduceRisk: Adhere strictly to prescribed maintenance biologic therapies (anti-TNF, IL-12/23, JAK inhibitors)
Complete smoking cessation (essential for Crohn’s disease patients to reduce surgical recurrence)
Undergo regular surveillance colonoscopies starting 8 years after IBD diagnosis to screen for colorectal dysplasia
Avoid regular NSAID usage which triggers disease flares
whenToSeeDoctor: Frequent bloody diarrhea lasting more than a few days
Severe abdominal pain accompanied by high fever and inability to pass gas (toxic megacolon / obstruction)
Development of an anal fissure, abscess, or draining perianal fistula (Crohn’s)
Rapid, unintended weight loss accompanied by chronic exhaustion
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects nearly 7 million people worldwide, with rapidly accelerating prevalence across newly industrialized nations.
reliableSources: Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation Clinical Guidelines
European Crohn’s and Colitis Organisation (ECCO) Guidelines
American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) IBD Technical Reviews

diseases.name: Gallstones
diseases.shortDescription: Hardened deposits of digestive fluid that can form in your gallbladder, causing intense upper abdominal pain when blocking bile ducts.
diseases.whatIsIt: Gallstones (cholelithiasis) are solid crystalline concretions formed in the gallbladder. Cholesterol gallstones (80%–90%) form when bile contains excessive cholesterol that supersaturates and crystallizes. If a stone lodges in the cystic duct, it causes severe biliary colic and acute cholecystitis.
whyDoesItHappen: Excess cholesterol secretion by the liver supersaturating gallbladder bile
Incomplete or infrequent gallbladder emptying (gallbladder hypomotility / stasis)
Excess bilirubin in bile (pigment stones) resulting from hemolytic anemias or cirrhosis
Rapid significant weight loss, prolonged fasting, or total parenteral nutrition (TPN)
High estrogen levels (pregnancy, oral contraceptives) increasing biliary cholesterol saturation
signsYouMayNotice: Biliary colic: sudden, rapidly intensifying pain in the upper right abdomen or center of abdomen
Pain radiating to the right shoulder blade, right shoulder, or middle back
Pain typically starts 30 to 60 minutes after eating a fatty, greasy meal and lasts 1 to 5 hours
Nausea, belching, and vomiting during acute pain episodes
If complicated by cholecystitis: constant severe right upper quadrant pain with fever and chills
If complicated by common bile duct blockage (choledocholithiasis): yellowing of skin and eyes (jaundice) and dark tea-colored urine
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable metabolic and biliary tract disorder.
whoIsAtRisk: The "Four Fs": Female, Forty (or older), Fertile (multiparity/estrogen), and Fat (overweight/obese)
Individuals of Native American or Hispanic descent (high genetic predisposition)
People who have undergone rapid bariatric weight loss
howToReduceRisk: Maintain a healthy weight through gradual, steady weight loss (no more than 1 to 2 lbs per week)
Consume high-fiber foods (oats, legumes, vegetables) and healthy unsaturated fats (olive oil, nuts)
Avoid crash diets and prolonged starvation which cause gallbladder bile stasis
whenToSeeDoctor: Abdominal pain so intense that you cannot sit still or find a comfortable position
Severe right upper abdominal pain accompanied by high fever and shaking chills
Yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes (jaundice)
Clay-colored (pale) stools and dark urine
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects 10% to 15% of the adult population in Western countries; roughly 20% of carriers develop symptomatic biliary colic.
reliableSources: Tokyo Guidelines (TG18) for Management of Acute Cholecystitis
American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) Clinical Guideline on Focal Liver and Biliary Lesions
World Journal of Emergency Surgery (WSES) Cholecystitis Guidelines

diseases.name: Celiac Disease
diseases.shortDescription: An autoimmune condition where eating gluten triggers an immune reaction that damages the lining of the small intestine.
diseases.whatIsIt: Celiac disease is a chronic systemic autoimmune enteropathy triggered by the ingestion of gluten (proteins found in wheat, rye, and barley) in genetically susceptible individuals carrying HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8. The resulting immune response flattens intestinal villi (villous atrophy), causing nutrient malabsorption.
whyDoesItHappen: Deamidation of gluten gliadin peptides by tissue transglutaminase (tTG)
Presentation of deamidated gliadin to CD4+ T cells by HLA-DQ2/DQ8 heterodimers
Release of pro-inflammatory cytokines causing intraepithelial lymphocytosis and villous blunting
Loss of brush-border absorptive surface area leading to malabsorption of iron, calcium, folate, and fat-soluble vitamins
signsYouMayNotice: Chronic diarrhea, pale, foul-smelling, fatty floating stools (steatorrhea)
Persistent abdominal bloating, gas, distension, and vague cramping
Iron-deficiency anemia that does not respond to oral iron supplements
Unexplained weight loss, stunted growth, and delayed puberty in children
Dermatitis herpetiformis: an intensely itchy, blistering skin rash appearing symmetrically on elbows, knees, and buttocks
Early-onset osteopenia or osteoporosis from chronic calcium malabsorption
Chronic fatigue, recurring mouth canker sores (aphthous stomatitis), and neurological tingling (neuropathy)
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable autoimmune disorder driven by dietary gluten exposure in genetically predisposed individuals.
whoIsAtRisk: Individuals with a first-degree relative with celiac disease (1 in 10 risk)
People with Type 1 Diabetes, autoimmune thyroiditis, Down syndrome, or Turner syndrome
howToReduceRisk: The only effective medical treatment is a 100% strict, lifelong gluten-free diet (eliminating all wheat, barley, rye, and cross-contaminated oats)
Do NOT start a gluten-free diet before diagnostic antibody testing (tTG-IgA) and duodenal biopsy, or tests will become falsely negative
Read food labels diligently for hidden gluten in sauces, processed meats, medications, and seasonings
whenToSeeDoctor: Chronic diarrhea or bloating lasting more than 2 weeks
Unexplained iron deficiency anemia or failure to gain weight in children
Intensely itchy, blistering rash on elbows, knees, or buttocks
Family member diagnosed with celiac disease (recommended screening)
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects approximately 1% of the world’s population; however, up to 70% to 80% of individuals remain undiagnosed.
reliableSources: American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) Clinical Guidelines on Celiac Disease
European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition (ESPGHAN)
Celiac Disease Foundation

diseases.name: Pancreatitis
diseases.shortDescription: Inflammation of the pancreas that occurs when digestive enzymes become activated inside the pancreas, causing autodigestion.
diseases.whatIsIt: Pancreatitis occurs when digestive enzymes (trypsinogen) activate prematurely within pancreatic acinar cells rather than in the duodenum. This triggers autodigestion of pancreatic parenchyma, vascular thrombosis, and local necrosis, which can escalate into systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS).
whyDoesItHappen: Gallstones (responsible for 40%–50% of acute cases) obstructing the ampulla of Vater
Heavy alcohol consumption (responsible for 30% of acute cases and most chronic cases)
Severe hypertriglyceridemia (serum triglyceride levels >1,000 mg/dL)
Medications (azathioprine, valproic acid, thiazides) and endoscopic procedures (ERCP)
Autoimmune pancreatitis, genetic mutations (PRSS1, CFTR), and abdominal trauma
signsYouMayNotice: Sudden, severe, boring pain in the upper abdomen (epigastrium) that radiates directly through to the back
Pain that feels worse after eating, especially fatty foods, and is partially relieved by leaning forward
Nausea and repeated vomiting that does not relieve the abdominal pain
Rapid pulse (tachycardia), low-grade fever, and swollen, tender abdomen
In chronic pancreatitis: recurrent abdominal pain, severe weight loss, oily foul-smelling stools (steatorrhea), and secondary diabetes
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable acute and chronic inflammatory disease.
whoIsAtRisk: People with gallstones who have not undergone cholecystectomy
Heavy regular consumers of alcohol
Individuals with severe untreated hypertriglyceridemia
howToReduceRisk: Undergo prompt laparoscopic gallbladder removal (cholecystectomy) after a first episode of gallstone pancreatitis
Completely eliminate alcohol consumption, particularly if diagnosed with a prior pancreatitis attack
Maintain serum triglycerides below 500 mg/dL through dietary modifications and fibrates
whenToSeeDoctor: EMERGENCY: Immediate emergency hospitalization for severe, unyielding upper abdominal pain radiating to the back
Abdominal pain accompanied by rapid breathing, cold clammy skin, or confusion (hypovolemic shock)
Yellowing of skin or eyes (jaundice) accompanying pancreatic pain
diseases.howCommonIsIt: One of the most frequent gastrointestinal reasons for emergency hospital admission, with an incidence of 34 cases per 100,000 annually.
reliableSources: American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) Guideline: Management of Acute Pancreatitis
Revised Atlanta Classification of Acute Pancreatitis
International Association of Pancreatology (IAP) / APA Guidelines

diseases.name: Kidney Stones
diseases.shortDescription: Hard mineral deposits that form inside your kidneys and cause intense, spasmodic flank pain when passing through the urinary tract.
diseases.whatIsIt: Kidney stones (nephrolithiasis) are crystalline mineral deposits that precipitate in renal calyces and pelvis. Calcium oxalate stones account for ~80% of all cases; others include uric acid, struvite (infection stones), and cystine. As a stone dislodges and descends into the narrow ureter, it causes ureteral spasm and acute hydronephrosis.
whyDoesItHappen: Inadequate daily fluid intake leading to concentrated urine and solute supersaturation
Excessive urinary excretion of calcium (hypercalciuria), oxalate, or uric acid
Low levels of urinary stone inhibitors, especially citrate (hypocitraturia)
Diets high in sodium (promotes renal calcium dumping), animal protein, and high-oxalate foods (spinach, almonds)
Metabolic conditions: primary hyperparathyroidism, gout, obesity, and gastric bypass surgery
signsYouMayNotice: Renal colic: agonizing, sharp, spasmodic pain in the flank (side and back below the ribs)
Pain that waves and radiates downward into the lower abdomen, groin, and testicle or labia
Inability to lie still: patients pace or writhe trying to find relief
Hematuria: pink, red, or brownish blood in the urine
Dysuria: painful or burning urination, accompanied by a constant urgent need to urinate
Nausea and vomiting induced by visceral splanchnic nerve stimulation
Cloudy or foul-smelling urine if a secondary urinary tract infection is present
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable metabolic and urological crystal formation.
whoIsAtRisk: Individuals who do not drink enough water throughout the day or work in hot, dehydrating environments
People with a personal or family history of kidney stones (recurrence rate is 50% within 5 years)
Individuals with gout, inflammatory bowel disease, or hyperparathyroidism
howToReduceRisk: Drink enough water to produce at least 2.5 liters of clear, pale urine daily
Limit dietary sodium to <2,000 mg/day (reducing urinary calcium concentration)
Maintain normal dietary calcium intake (calcium binds oxalate in the intestine, preventing absorption)
Add fresh lemon or lime juice to drinking water to boost urinary citrate levels
whenToSeeDoctor: EMERGENCY: Flank pain accompanied by high fever and chills (infection behind an obstructed stone is life-threatening urosepsis)
Pain so severe that you cannot sit still, manage pain, or keep fluids down
Blood in your urine or difficulty passing urine (anuria requires urgent intervention)
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects roughly 1 in 10 people over their lifetime, with incidence rising globally alongside temperatures and obesity.
reliableSources: American Urological Association (AUA) / Endourological Society Stone Guidelines
European Association of Urology (EAU) Urolithiasis Guidelines
National Kidney Foundation (NKF)

diseases.name: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)
diseases.medicalName: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH / Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms)
diseases.shortDescription: A non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate gland in older men that squeezes the urethra, causing urinary difficulties.
diseases.whatIsIt: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) is an age-associated non-malignant proliferation of stromal and glandular epithelial cells within the transition zone of the prostate gland. Because the prostate surrounds the proximal urethra, its enlargement creates bladder outlet obstruction (BOO).
whyDoesItHappen: Accumulation of dihydrotestosterone (DHT) in the prostate gland catalyzed by the enzyme 5-alpha-reductase
