Age-dependent increase in the ratio of estrogen to testosterone stimulating prostatic cellular hyperplasia
Dysregulation of local growth factors (FGF, TGF-beta) and decreased apoptosis
Chronic pelvic ischemia and metabolic syndrome accelerating prostatic tissue enlargement
signsYouMayNotice: Weak, interrupted, or hesitant urinary stream (hesitancy)
Nocturia: waking up two or more times at night to urinate, disrupting restorative sleep
Urinary frequency: feeling the need to urinate every 1 to 2 hours throughout the day
Urinary urgency: sudden, compelling urge to urinate that is difficult to postpone
Straining or pushing to begin and maintain urination
Feeling that the bladder has not emptied completely after urination (residual urine)
Post-void dribbling of urine onto clothing
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable age-related endocrine and urological disorder. BPH is NOT prostate cancer and does not turn into cancer.
whoIsAtRisk: Men aged 50 and older (present in 50% of men in their 50s and up to 80%–90% of men in their 80s)
Men with obesity, metabolic syndrome, or lack of regular physical exercise
Family history of benign prostatic enlargement
howToReduceRisk: Avoid drinking large volumes of fluids in the evening, especially within 2 hours of bedtime
Limit evening caffeine and alcohol consumption, which act as diuretics and bladder irritants
Avoid over-the-counter decongestants (pseudoephedrine) and antihistamines which tighten the bladder neck
Take prescribed medications: alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin) to relax the prostate capsule, or 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride) to shrink prostate volume
whenToSeeDoctor: EMERGENCY: Complete inability to pass urine (acute urinary retention requires emergency bladder catheterization)
Visible blood in the urine (gross hematuria)
Painful urination accompanied by fever and chills (prostatitis or ascending urinary infection)
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Extremely common; affects an estimated 100 million men worldwide, making it one of the leading conditions managed in urology clinics.
reliableSources: American Urological Association (AUA) Management of Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms Attributed to BPH
European Association of Urology (EAU) Non-neurogenic Male LUTS Guidelines
National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK)

diseases.name: Nephrotic Syndrome
diseases.medicalName: Nephrotic Syndrome & Glomerulonephritis (Podocyte Filtration Barrier Defect)
diseases.shortDescription: A kidney disorder that causes your body to pass too much protein in your urine, resulting in severe whole-body swelling.
diseases.whatIsIt: Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by heavy proteinuria (>3.5 grams per 24 hours), severe hypoalbuminemia (<3.0 g/dL), peripheral edema, and hyperlipidemia. It results from damage to glomerular podocytes and slit diaphragms, which normally prevent plasma albumin from escaping into urine.
whyDoesItHappen: Primary glomerular diseases: Minimal Change Disease (most common in children), Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), and Membranous Nephropathy
Secondary glomerular diseases: Diabetic nephropathy, Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (lupus nephritis), and amyloidosis
Infections such as Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, HIV, and malaria
Adverse drug reactions to NSAIDs, gold salts, or lithium
signsYouMayNotice: Severe swelling (edema), especially around the eyes in the morning (periorbital edema)
Pitting edema in ankles, feet, and lower legs that leaves an indentation when pressed
Ascites (abdominal swelling) causing clothes to feel tight and abdominal fullness
Foamy or frothy urine resembling beer foam caused by high protein content
Unintended rapid weight gain from fluid retention (often 10–20 pounds within weeks)
Fatigue, poor appetite, and high susceptibility to bacterial infections due to loss of protective immunoglobulins in urine
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable autoimmune, metabolic, and glomerular filtration disorder.
whoIsAtRisk: Children aged 2 to 6 years (predisposed to Minimal Change Disease)
Adults with long-standing diabetes or autoimmune diseases (lupus)
Individuals with chronic viral infections (HIV, Hepatitis B/C)
howToReduceRisk: Maintain strict low-sodium dietary intake (<1,500 mg daily) to minimize fluid accumulation
Use ACE inhibitors or ARBs to reduce intraglomerular pressure and decrease urinary protein loss
Follow prescribed corticosteroid (prednisone) or immunosuppressive protocols to induce remission
whenToSeeDoctor: Noticeable puffiness around the eyes or sudden swelling of the feet and legs
Persistent foamy urine noticed during daily voiding
Sudden severe unilateral leg pain or swelling (nephrotic patients have high risk of deep vein thrombosis due to loss of antithrombin III)
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects approximately 3 in 100,000 children and 3 in 100,000 adults each year worldwide.
reliableSources: Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Glomerular Diseases Guideline
International Pediatric Nephrology Association (IPNA)
National Kidney Foundation (NKF)

diseases.name: Viral Hepatitis (Hep B & C)
diseases.medicalName: Chronic Viral Hepatitis B & C (HBV / HCV Hepatosplenic Infection)
diseases.shortDescription: Infections of the liver caused by the Hepatitis B and C viruses that can lead to chronic liver scarring (cirrhosis) and liver cancer.
diseases.whatIsIt: Hepatitis B (a DNA hepadnavirus) and Hepatitis C (an RNA flavivirus) are blood-borne viruses that chronically infect hepatocytes. While acute infection can cause self-limited jaundice, chronic persistent infection leads to ongoing immune-mediated liver necrosis, fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma.
whyDoesItHappen: Hepatitis B: transmission through perinatal mother-to-child contact, unprotected sexual intercourse, or contaminated injection equipment
Hepatitis C: transmission predominantly through blood-to-blood contact (unsterile needle sharing, unscreened transfusions, non-sterile tattoo instruments)
Inadequate host T-cell immune clearance allowing the virus to establish chronic intrahepatic infection
signsYouMayNotice: Chronic cases are often entirely asymptomatic for decades ("the silent epidemic")
Gradual onset of persistent, unexplained fatigue and low energy
Mild right upper quadrant abdominal discomfort over the liver
During acute flares or advanced cirrhosis: jaundice (yellow skin/eyes), dark tea-colored urine, and clay-colored stools
Loss of appetite, nausea, and joint and muscle aches
Late cirrhosis signs: fluid in abdomen (ascites), spider angiomas on skin, and vomiting blood from esophageal varices
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Blood and body fluids. Hep B: mother-to-baby at birth, sexual contact, blood. Hep C: direct blood-to-blood contact. Cannot spread through casual contact, sneezing, hugging, or sharing food.
whoIsAtRisk: Individuals born to Hepatitis B-positive mothers who did not receive infant immunoprophylaxis
People who inject drugs or share needles/syringes
Individuals who received blood transfusions before routine screening began (1992 in Western nations)
Healthcare workers exposed to accidental needle-stick injuries
howToReduceRisk: Receive the Hepatitis B vaccine series (available for all infants and adults; >95% protective)
Hepatitis C has NO vaccine, but can be 100% CURED in 8 to 12 weeks with oral Direct-Acting Antivirals (DAAs)
Never share needles, syringes, razors, or toothbrushes
Ensure all tattoo and piercing studios use single-use, sterile disposable equipment
whenToSeeDoctor: Yellowing of skin or whites of eyes (jaundice)
Anyone who has ever injected drugs, even once, should undergo one-time Hepatitis C antibody screening
Pregnant women should be screened for Hepatitis B at the first prenatal visit to protect the infant
Unexplained elevated liver enzymes (ALT / AST) discovered on routine blood work
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Over 350 million people worldwide live with chronic Hepatitis B or C; responsible for over 1.1 million deaths annually from cirrhosis and liver cancer.
reliableSources: World Health Organization (WHO) Global Hepatitis Report
AASLD / IDSA HCV Guidance: Recommendations for Testing, Managing, and Treating Hepatitis C
European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL) Clinical Practice Guidelines

diseases.name: HIV / AIDS
diseases.medicalName: Human Immunodeficiency Virus Infection (Retroviral CD4+ T-Cell Depletion)
diseases.shortDescription: A virus that attacks the body’s immune system, specifically CD4 T cells, which if untreated can lead to Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS).
diseases.whatIsIt: HIV is a human retrovirus (lentivirus) that infects CD4+ helper T-lymphocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells. By integrating its viral DNA into the host genome, it gradually destroys the cellular immune defense, leaving the patient vulnerable to life-threatening opportunistic infections and AIDS-defining malignancies.
whyDoesItHappen: Transmission of HIV-1 or HIV-2 through contact with infected blood, semen, pre-seminal fluid, rectal fluids, vaginal fluids, or breast milk
Unprotected condomless sexual intercourse (vaginal or anal)
Sharing needles, syringes, or other drug preparation equipment
Perinatal transmission from mother to child during pregnancy, birth, or breastfeeding without antiretroviral therapy
signsYouMayNotice: Acute retroviral syndrome (2 to 4 weeks after exposure): flu-like illness with fever, sore throat, generalized swollen lymph nodes, and a faint macular rash
Clinical latency stage: often zero symptoms for 8 to 10 years while viral replication continues
Progressive symptomatic stage: recurring oral thrush (Candida patches in mouth), chronic persistent diarrhea, oral hairy leukoplakia, and night sweats
Advanced AIDS (CD4 < 200 cells/uL): rapid unexplained weight loss ("wasting syndrome"), recurring severe pneumonia (Pneumocystis jirovecii), Kaposi sarcoma skin lesions, and severe chronic fatigue
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Specific body fluids (blood, semen, vaginal secretions, breast milk). Cannot spread through saliva, sweat, tears, toilet seats, hugging, or mosquito bites.
whoIsAtRisk: Individuals with multiple sexual partners without barrier protection
People who share needles or syringes for drug use
Individuals with other untreated sexually transmitted infections (which increase transmission risk)
howToReduceRisk: U=U (Undetectable = Untransmittable): individuals on Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) with undetectable viral loads CANNOT transmit HIV sexually
Take Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) if at ongoing risk; take Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) within 72 hours of an accidental exposure
Consistent and correct use of latex or polyurethane condoms during sexual intercourse
Use sterile single-use injection equipment through needle-exchange programs
whenToSeeDoctor: Anyone who has had a potential exposure within the past 72 hours should seek PEP immediately at an emergency room or clinic
Fever, sore throat, and swollen lymph nodes 2 to 4 weeks after a high-risk encounter
Routine annual HIV testing is recommended by the CDC for all individuals aged 13 to 64
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Over 39 million people globally live with HIV; modern once-daily ART regimens allow individuals to live long, healthy, normal lifespans.
reliableSources: UNAIDS Global HIV & AIDS Statistics Factsheet
CDC HIV Guidelines and Surveillance
World Health Organization (WHO) HIV / AIDS Key Facts

diseases.name: Chikungunya
diseases.shortDescription: A mosquito-borne viral disease that causes sudden high fever and severe, often debilitating joint pain that can last for months.
diseases.whatIsIt: Chikungunya is an arboviral infection transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. The name comes from the Makonde language meaning "that which bends up," referring to the stooped posture of patients suffering from its signature excruciating polyarthralgia.
whyDoesItHappen: Bite of infected female Aedes aegypti or Aedes albopictus mosquitoes (daytime biters)
Viral replication in synovial macrophages, fibroblasts, and periosteal tissue causing intense local cytokine storm
signsYouMayNotice: Abrupt onset of high fever (often >102°F or 39°C) lasting 3 to 7 days
Severe, incapacitating joint pain (arthralgia) affecting multiple joints symmetrically (wrists, ankles, knuckles, knees)
Visible swelling in hands, feet, and ankles with profound joint stiffness in the morning
Maculopapular rash spreading across trunk and limbs roughly 2 to 5 days after fever starts
Headache, muscle aches, back pain, nausea, and severe fatigue
Chronic phase: joint pain and morning stiffness persisting for months or even years in up to 40% of patients
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Vector-borne through mosquito bites. Does not spread person-to-person through touch or saliva.
whoIsAtRisk: Residents and travelers in tropical and subtropical regions of South Asia, Southeast Asia, Africa, and the Americas
Older adults over 65 and individuals with pre-existing joint disease (higher risk of chronic arthralgia)
howToReduceRisk: Apply mosquito repellents containing DEET, Picaridin, or Oil of Lemon Eucalyptus (OLE) to exposed skin
Empty, drain, or cover containers that hold standing water (flower pots, buckets, tires) to eliminate mosquito breeding sites
Wear long-sleeved light-colored clothing and stay in rooms with air conditioning or secure window screens
Recently approved chikungunya vaccines (Ixchiq) are available for high-risk travelers and endemic populations
whenToSeeDoctor: Sudden high fever combined with severe joint pain and swelling, especially after tropical travel
Inability to walk or perform basic daily self-care due to extreme joint pain
Severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, or cold extremities
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Causes major explosive epidemics across tropical regions; millions of cases have been recorded across the Americas and Asia.
reliableSources: World Health Organization (WHO) Chikungunya Factsheet
CDC Chikungunya Virus Information for Healthcare Providers
PAHO / WHO Chikungunya Guidelines

diseases.name: Influenza (The Flu)
diseases.medicalName: Seasonal Influenza (Influenza Virus A & B Tracheobronchitis)
diseases.shortDescription: A contagious viral infection of the respiratory passages causing acute fever, severe muscle aches, chills, and fatigue.
diseases.whatIsIt: Influenza is an acute respiratory infection caused by Influenza A and B viruses. Unlike the common cold, flu strikes abruptly with high fever, severe body-wide myalgias, and systemic toxicity, and can trigger life-threatening secondary bacterial pneumonia in vulnerable populations.
whyDoesItHappen: Infection by Influenza A (H1N1, H3N2) or Influenza B viruses
Frequent antigenic drift (point mutations in viral surface hemagglutinin and neuraminidase proteins) necessitating annual vaccine updates
Inhalation of infectious viral aerosols generated by infected individuals coughing, sneezing, or speaking
signsYouMayNotice: Sudden, abrupt onset of high fever (100.4°F to 104°F / 38°C to 40°C) and violent shaking chills
Severe, debilitating muscle aches and body aches (myalgias), especially in the back and legs
Profound, overwhelming exhaustion and fatigue that forces you to stay in bed
Dry, painful, hacking cough and burning throat discomfort
Severe headache, pain behind the eyes, and nasal congestion
Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea (more common in children than adults)
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Rapid airborne transmission through tiny droplets and aerosols; highly contagious in schools, workplaces, and public transit.
whoIsAtRisk: Adults aged 65 and older and infants and young children under 2 years
Pregnant women (higher risk of severe respiratory complications and hospitalization)
Individuals with asthma, heart failure, diabetes, or immunosuppression
howToReduceRisk: Get an annual influenza vaccination every autumn (reduces flu illness, medical visits, and hospitalizations)
Wash hands frequently with soap and water or use an alcohol-based hand rub
Stay home when sick for at least 24 hours after fever is gone without fever-reducing medicine
Initiate prescription neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir / Tamiflu) or baloxavir within 48 hours of onset if high-risk
whenToSeeDoctor: Difficulty breathing, shortness of breath, or chest pain
Fever or cough that improves but then returns or worsens significantly (suggests secondary bacterial pneumonia)
Dizziness, confusion, or inability to keep fluids down
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Causes an estimated 1 billion infections, 3 to 5 million severe illnesses, and 290,000 to 650,000 respiratory deaths worldwide annually.
reliableSources: World Health Organization (WHO) Influenza (Seasonal) Factsheet
CDC Influenza Clinical Information and Weekly Surveillance
Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) Influenza Guidelines

diseases.name: Cholera
diseases.shortDescription: An acute, severe diarrheal illness caused by infection of the intestine with Vibrio cholerae bacteria, capable of causing fatal dehydration within hours.
diseases.whatIsIt: Cholera is a severe secretory diarrheal disease caused by ingesting food or water contaminated with Vibrio cholerae (serogroups O1 and O139). The bacterium releases cholera toxin (CTX), which causes massive, uninhibited secretion of water and electrolytes into the small intestinal lumen, producing characteristic painless "rice-water stools."
whyDoesItHappen: Ingestion of water or food contaminated with feces from an infected person
Inadequate municipal sewage infrastructure, flooding, humanitarian crises, and contaminated community water sources
Cholera toxin binding to GM1 ganglioside receptors on intestinal enterocytes, activating adenylate cyclase and pumping massive chloride and water into the bowel
signsYouMayNotice: Sudden onset of profuse, painless, watery diarrhea that resembles cloudy rice-water (can exceed 1 liter per hour)
Vomiting accompanying rapid fluid loss
Severe dehydration: sunken eyes, dry mouth, extreme thirst, cold clammy skin, and loss of skin elasticity (skin turgor takes >2 seconds to recoil)
Severe, painful muscle cramps in legs and abdomen caused by rapid electrolyte depletion (potassium and sodium loss)
Hypovolemic shock: rapid, weak pulse, unmeasurable blood pressure, and absence of urination (anuria)
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Fecal-oral route through contaminated drinking water supplies and street-vended food in unsanitary environments.
whoIsAtRisk: Residents of refugee camps, conflict zones, and areas lacking clean tap water and sanitized toilets
Individuals with blood group O (higher risk of severe dehydration from cholera)
People with low stomach acid (hypochlorhydria)
howToReduceRisk: Drink only safe, boiled, or chemically treated chlorinated water; drink bottled beverages with intact seals
Follow the rule: "Boil it, cook it, peel it, or forget it" for food consumed in outbreak areas
Administer Oral Cholera Vaccines (OCV: Shanchol, Euvichol) in endemic regions and humanitarian emergencies
Wash hands thoroughly with soap after using the toilet and before preparing food
whenToSeeDoctor: EMERGENCY: Immediate emergency medical treatment for profuse watery diarrhea in an outbreak region
Signs of severe dehydration: inability to drink, lethargy, sunken eyes, and absence of urination (requires immediate IV Ringer’s lactate)
Begin drinking Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) solution immediately while traveling to a healthcare facility
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Causes an estimated 1.3 to 4.0 million cases and 21,000 to 143,000 deaths worldwide annually according to the WHO.
reliableSources: World Health Organization (WHO) Cholera Factsheet & Global Task Force on Cholera Control (GTFCC)
CDC Cholera Clinical Guidance
Doctors Without Borders (MSF) Cholera Outbreak Guidelines

diseases.name: Sepsis
diseases.medicalName: Sepsis & Septic Shock (Dysregulated Host Immune Response to Infection)
diseases.shortDescription: A life-threatening medical emergency caused by the body’s overwhelming and toxic response to an underlying infection, leading to tissue damage and organ failure.
diseases.whatIsIt: Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection (SOFA score increase >= 2). When the body’s infection-fighting chemicals trigger widespread systemic inflammation, microvascular blood clots form and capillaries leak, starving vital organs of oxygen and causing multi-organ failure.
whyDoesItHappen: Complication of an existing infection in the lungs (pneumonia), urinary tract (pyelonephritis), abdomen (peritonitis), or skin (cellulitis)
Bacterial pathogens (most common), fungal, or viral infections overwhelming local tissue defenses and entering the bloodstream (bacteremia)
Release of endotoxins and cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6) triggering massive systemic vasodilation and endothelial barrier collapse
Septic shock: profound cellular metabolic abnormalities and persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain mean arterial pressure >= 65 mmHg despite adequate fluid resuscitation
signsYouMayNotice: T - Temperature: higher or lower than normal (fever >101°F or hypothermia <96.8°F / 36°C)
I - Infection: signs of an underlying infection (productive cough, burning urination, red warm wound)
M - Mental decline: confused, sleepy, slurred speech, or difficult to rouse
E - Extremely ill: "I feel like I might die", severe body-wide pain or discomfort
Tachypnea (rapid breathing >22 breaths/min) and tachycardia (racing heart rate >90 bpm)
Mottled, bluish, or pale skin with cold extremities, and absence of urination for over 8 to 12 hours
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Sepsis itself is not contagious; however, the initial underlying infection (pneumonia, meningitis, flu) can be transmitted.
whoIsAtRisk: Adults aged 65 and older and infants under 1 year of age
People with weakened immune systems (chemotherapy, diabetes, cirrhosis, asplenia)
Hospitalized, ICU, or recently operated patients with indwelling catheters or IV lines
howToReduceRisk: Treat all bacterial infections (UTIs, skin wounds, pneumonia) promptly under medical supervision
Stay up to date on recommended vaccinations (flu, pneumonia, COVID-19)
Practice clean wound hygiene: wash cuts and scrapes immediately with soap and water and keep them covered
whenToSeeDoctor: EMERGENCY: Immediate emergency medical dispatch (911 / 108) if an infected patient develops confusion, rapid breathing, and severe weakness
High fever or hypothermia combined with shivering and racing pulse
Absence of urination and mottled, discolored skin
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects an estimated 49 million people worldwide each year, resulting in 11 million deaths (1 in every 5 deaths globally is sepsis-related).
reliableSources: Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) International Guidelines 2026
World Health Organization (WHO) Sepsis Factsheet
Sepsis Alliance Clinical Guidelines

diseases.name: Osteoarthritis
diseases.shortDescription: The most common form of arthritis, caused by the gradual wear and breakdown of protective cartilage on the ends of your bones.
diseases.whatIsIt: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a progressive whole-joint disease characterized by breakdown of articular hyaline cartilage, subchondral bone remodeling, osteophyte (bone spur) formation, and synovial low-grade inflammation, commonly affecting the knees, hips, hands, and cervical/lumbar spine.
whyDoesItHappen: Mechanical joint overload and repetitive micro-trauma exceeding the repair capacity of chondrocytes
Aging: chondrocyte senescence and loss of proteoglycans leading to cartilage dehydration and cracking
Prior joint injuries (torn meniscus, anterior cruciate ligament tears, intra-articular fractures)
Obesity: mechanical joint stress combined with adipokine-driven systemic low-grade inflammation
Genetic predisposition affecting cartilage matrix proteins (collagen type II)
signsYouMayNotice: Joint pain during or after movement that improves with rest
Joint stiffness noticed upon waking up in the morning or after periods of inactivity, resolving within 30 minutes
Crepitus: a grating, crackling, or grinding sensation when moving the joint
Loss of joint flexibility and reduced range of motion
Bony enlargements on finger joints: Heberden’s nodes (distal joints) and Bouchard’s nodes (middle joints)
Joint tenderness and mild localized swelling without warm redness
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable progressive degenerative and biomechanical joint disease.
whoIsAtRisk: Individuals aged 50 and older (prevalence rises steeply with age)
Women (more common and severe in women than men, especially after menopause)
People with obesity (each pound of excess weight adds 4 pounds of pressure across knees)
Athletes and workers with repetitive heavy lifting or kneeling jobs
howToReduceRisk: Maintain a healthy body weight to reduce mechanical load across knee and hip cartilage
Engage in low-impact physical activities (swimming, cycling, water aerobics, brisk walking)
Strengthen quadriceps and gluteal muscles to provide shock absorption for the knee and hip joints
Use assistive devices (walking cane in contralateral hand, knee braces) to optimize joint mechanics
whenToSeeDoctor: Joint pain or stiffness that interferes with walking, climbing stairs, or sleeping
Sudden swelling, redness, and heat in a joint (requires evaluation to rule out infection or gout)
Joint that gives way or locks, preventing complete extension
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects over 528 million people worldwide, representing the leading cause of disability in older adults.
reliableSources: OARSI (Osteoarthritis Research Society International) Guidelines
American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Guideline for the Management of OA of the Hand, Hip, and Knee
CDC Osteoarthritis Overview

diseases.name: Rheumatoid Arthritis
diseases.shortDescription: A chronic autoimmune disease where your immune system attacks the synovium lining your joints, causing painful swelling and bone erosion.
diseases.whatIsIt: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) is a systemic inflammatory autoimmune condition characterized by symmetric peripheral polyarthritis. Autoantibodies (Rheumatoid Factor and anti-citrullinated protein antibodies / ACPA) drive chronic synovial hyperproliferation (pannus formation), which invades and destroys adjacent articular cartilage and bone.
whyDoesItHappen: Autoimmune attack driven by autoreactive CD4+ T cells, B cells, and inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-6)
Genetic susceptibility involving HLA-DRB1 shared epitope alleles
Environmental trigger: tobacco smoking strongly interacts with HLA genes to induce citrullination of mucosal antigens
Periodontal bacterial pathogens (Porphyromonas gingivalis) producing bacterial peptidylarginine deiminase
signsYouMayNotice: Symmetric joint pain and swelling: affects the same joints on both sides of the body (both wrists, both sets of knuckles)
Prolonged morning joint stiffness lasting greater than 60 minutes before gradually loosening up
Small joints of hands (MCP and PIP joints) and feet (MTP joints) are characteristically affected first
Joints feel warm, tender, and puffy or "spongy" to the touch
Systemic symptoms: persistent fatigue, low-grade fevers, loss of appetite, and weight loss
Advanced signs: rheumatoid nodules under the skin over bony pressure points, ulnar deviation of fingers, and swan-neck deformities
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable systemic autoimmune condition.
whoIsAtRisk: Women (two to three times more likely to develop RA than men)
Onset typically occurs between ages 30 and 55
Cigarette smokers with genetic predisposition
Individuals with a family history of autoimmune diseases
howToReduceRisk: Quit smoking immediately (the most important modifiable risk factor for developing and worsening RA)
Treat-to-target: initiate Disease-Modifying Anti-Rheumatic Drugs (DMARDs: methotrexate, biologics, JAK inhibitors) as early as possible to prevent irreversible joint erosion and disability
Practice good dental hygiene to prevent periodontal bacterial inflammation
whenToSeeDoctor: Persistent swelling and tenderness in multiple joints lasting more than 2 to 3 weeks
Morning joint stiffness that takes more than an hour to improve
Joint symptoms accompanied by unexplained fever and profound fatigue
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects approximately 18 million people worldwide (roughly 0.5% to 1% of the adult population).
reliableSources: American College of Rheumatology (ACR) / EULAR Classification Criteria for Rheumatoid Arthritis
European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) RA Guidelines
Arthritis Foundation Clinical Overview

diseases.name: Lupus (SLE)
diseases.shortDescription: A complex chronic autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks tissues across multiple organs, including skin, joints, kidneys, and brain.
diseases.whatIsIt: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is the prototypical systemic autoimmune disease. Defective clearance of apoptotic cellular debris leads to the generation of antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA). Immune complexes deposit in microvascular capillary beds, activating complement and damaging multiple organ systems.
whyDoesItHappen: Impaired clearance of apoptotic cell nuclei exposing nuclear antigens to the immune system
B-cell hyperactivity and generation of pathogenic autoantibodies (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith)
Genetic susceptibility involving over 100 loci affecting type I interferon signaling (IFN-alpha)
Environmental triggers: ultraviolet (UV) sunlight radiation inducing keratinocyte apoptosis and disease flares
Female sex hormones (estrogen promotes immune reactivity, explaining the strong female predominance)
signsYouMayNotice: Malar rash: a butterfly-shaped red rash across the bridge of the nose and cheeks, sparing the nasolabial folds
Discoid rash: raised, red scaly patches that can leave scars and patchy scalp hair loss (alopecia)
Photosensitivity: skin rash or severe fatigue triggered by sun or UV light exposure
Painful, swollen joints (arthritis) affecting hands, wrists, and knees without permanent joint erosion
Pleuritic chest pain or shortness of breath from inflammation of heart or lung linings (pleuritis / pericarditis)
Kidney involvement (lupus nephritis): high blood pressure, foamy urine, and leg swelling
Profound, debilitating chronic fatigue, unexplained recurrent fevers, and painless oral/nasal ulcers
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable multisystem autoimmune disease.
whoIsAtRisk: Women of childbearing age (9 out of 10 people diagnosed with lupus are female, between ages 15 and 45)
Individuals of African, Hispanic/Latino, Asian, and Native American descent (higher incidence and severity)
People with a family history of lupus or other autoimmune conditions
howToReduceRisk: Strict sun and UV protection: wear broad-spectrum SPF 50+ sunscreen daily, wide-brimmed hats, and UV-protective clothing
Adhere strictly to prescribed hydroxychloroquine (Plaquenil), which reduces flares, organ damage, and mortality in all lupus patients
Manage stress, avoid smoking (which renders hydroxychloroquine ineffective), and get adequate rest
whenToSeeDoctor: New butterfly rash across cheeks and nose after sun exposure
New swelling in feet and ankles with frothy urine (signs of lupus nephritis)
Sharp chest pain that worsens when breathing in deeply or lying down flat
Sudden high fever, severe confusion, or seizures
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects an estimated 5 million people worldwide; with modern targeted therapies, 85% to 90% of patients have normal lifespans.
reliableSources: EULAR Recommendations for the Management of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
American College of Rheumatology (ACR) SLE Guidelines
Lupus Foundation of America

diseases.name: Fibromyalgia
diseases.medicalName: Fibromyalgia Syndrome (Central Pain Sensitization / Nociplastic Pain)
diseases.shortDescription: A disorder characterized by widespread musculoskeletal pain accompanied by fatigue, sleep, memory, and mood issues.
diseases.whatIsIt: Fibromyalgia is a condition of abnormal central pain processing (nociplastic pain). The central nervous system amplifies painful sensations by augmenting excitatory neurotransmitters (substance P, glutamate) and damping descending inhibitory pain pathways, turning non-painful stimuli into painful ones (allodynia).
whyDoesItHappen: Central sensitization: hyperexcitability of sensory neurons in the spinal dorsal horn and brain
Altered levels of neurotransmitters that regulate pain and mood (serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine)
Genetic predisposition influencing neuroendocrine and sensory pathways
Triggers: physical trauma (e.g. car accidents), chronic viral infections, emotional stress, or pre-existing chronic arthritis
signsYouMayNotice: Widespread musculoskeletal pain: dull, aching pain present on both sides of the body, above and below the waist, for at least 3 months
Hypersensitivity to touch or light pressure across multiple tender points
Chronic, unrefreshing sleep: waking up feeling exhausted even after sleeping 8 to 10 hours
Fibro fog: difficulties with focus, short-term memory, multitasking, and mental sharpness
Severe morning stiffness and headaches (tension headaches or migraines)
Co-occurring conditions: irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), painful bladder syndrome, and restless legs
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable neurosensory central sensitization syndrome.
whoIsAtRisk: Women (diagnosed roughly twice as often as men)
Middle-aged adults, though it can occur at any age
People with other rheumatic conditions (rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, osteoarthritis)
howToReduceRisk: Engage in regular low-impact aerobic exercise (walking, warm water aquatic exercise, gentle yoga)
Practice cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and mindfulness-based stress reduction
Maintain rigorous sleep hygiene to promote deep restorative slow-wave sleep
Avoid opioid painkillers (which do not work for nociplastic pain and can cause hyperalgesia)
whenToSeeDoctor: Widespread, persistent body aches lasting more than 3 months that disrupt daily activities
Severe unrefreshing sleep and cognitive difficulties affecting work performance
New joint swelling or redness (to ensure an inflammatory arthritis is not developing)
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects 2% to 4% of the global population (roughly 200 million people worldwide).
reliableSources: American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Fibromyalgia Diagnostic Criteria
EULAR Revised Recommendations for the Management of Fibromyalgia
National Fibromyalgia Association

diseases.name: Ankylosing Spondylitis
diseases.shortDescription: An inflammatory arthritis affecting the spine and large joints, which over time can cause small bones in the spine to fuse together.
diseases.whatIsIt: Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory seronegative spondyloarthropathy that primarily affects the sacroiliac joints and axial skeleton. Chronic inflammation at entheses (sites where tendons and ligaments attach to bone) leads to erosion, syndesmophyte formation, and eventual bony fusion ("bamboo spine").
whyDoesItHappen: Strong genetic association with the Human Leukocyte Antigen B27 (HLA-B27) gene (present in >90% of Caucasian patients)
Dysregulation of the IL-23 / IL-17 cytokine immune axis stimulating enthesitis and osteoproliferation
Altered gut mucosal microbiome interacting with genetic factors
signsYouMayNotice: Inflammatory back pain: dull, aching lower back and buttock pain that begins insidiously before age 45
Back stiffness that is worst in the morning or after resting, lasting >30 minutes and IMPROVING with exercise (not with rest)
Alternating buttock pain caused by sacroiliac joint inflammation
Chest wall pain and difficulty expanding the chest when taking deep breaths (costovertebral enthesitis)
Painful heel swelling (Achilles tendinitis or plantar fasciitis)
Acute anterior uveitis (eye inflammation): sudden onset of a red, painful eye with photophobia and blurred vision
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable genetic and autoimmune inflammatory arthritis.
whoIsAtRisk: Young men (men are more likely to develop severe spinal ankylosis; typical onset between ages 17 and 35)
Individuals who carry the HLA-B27 gene variant
Individuals with a family history of AS, psoriatic arthritis, or inflammatory bowel disease
howToReduceRisk: Engage in daily spinal stretching, posture exercises, and swimming to maintain spinal flexibility
Initiate early biologic therapies (TNF inhibitors or IL-17 inhibitors) to suppress inflammation and retard spinal fusion
Never smoke cigarettes; smoking accelerates syndesmophyte formation and irreversible spinal stiffening
whenToSeeDoctor: Persistent lower back pain that started before age 45, lasts >3 months, and improves with exercise but not rest
Sudden red, painful, light-sensitive eye (requires immediate ophthalmology evaluation for uveitis)
Severe stiffness in the morning that takes over an hour to loosen up
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects approximately 0.1% to 1.4% of the adult population depending on the regional prevalence of the HLA-B27 gene.
reliableSources: Assessment of SpondyloArthritis international Society (ASAS) / EULAR Guidelines
American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Axial Spondyloarthritis Guidelines
Spondylitis Association of America

diseases.name: Major Depressive Disorder
diseases.shortDescription: A common and serious mental health mood disorder that negatively affects how you feel, the way you think, and how you act.
diseases.whatIsIt: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is a biological, psychological, and social medical condition characterized by persistent depressed mood or loss of interest/pleasure (anhedonia) lasting at least 2 weeks. It impairs neurotransmitter signaling (serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine) in frontolimbic brain circuits and causes significant functional disability.
whyDoesItHappen: Neurochemical dysregulation in monoamine neurotransmitter systems and reduced neuroplasticity (BDNF deficiency)
Genetic vulnerability (heritability estimated around 35% to 40%)
Hyperactivity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis leading to sustained elevated cortisol levels
Psychological and environmental stressors: trauma, loss of a loved one, chronic medical illness, or financial distress
Chronic systemic low-grade inflammation affecting neurovascular function
signsYouMayNotice: Persistent feeling of sadness, emptiness, hopelessness, or tearfulness nearly every day
Marked loss of interest or pleasure in all or almost all activities once enjoyed (anhedonia)
Significant changes in appetite: weight loss or weight gain unrelated to dieting
Insomnia (especially early morning awakening) or excessive sleeping (hypersomnia)
Psychomotor agitation (restlessness) or psychomotor retardation (slowed speech and body movements)
Fatigue or loss of energy nearly every day, making basic tasks exhausting
Feelings of worthlessness or excessive, inappropriate guilt
Diminished ability to think, concentrate, or make simple everyday decisions
Recurrent thoughts of death, suicidal ideation, or suicide attempts
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable complex biopsychosocial mental health disorder.
whoIsAtRisk: Women (diagnosed roughly twice as often as men)
Individuals with a personal or family history of mood disorders
People experiencing major life transitions, social isolation, or chronic medical illness
Individuals with a history of childhood physical, emotional, or sexual trauma
howToReduceRisk: Seek evidence-based psychotherapy: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), Interpersonal Therapy (IPT), or Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT)
Adhere to prescribed antidepressant medications (SSRIs, SNRIs) as directed without stopping abruptly
Engage in regular aerobic physical activity, which stimulates brain neurogenesis and releases endorphins
Maintain strong social connections and practice structured sleep hygiene
whenToSeeDoctor: CRISIS / EMERGENCY: If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, call or text 988 (in the US/Canada) or local emergency services immediately
Symptoms of depression lasting continuously for more than two weeks
Inability to work, care for family members, or manage basic personal hygiene
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects an estimated 280 million people worldwide; the leading cause of disability among mental health disorders according to the WHO.
reliableSources: American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With MDD
World Health Organization (WHO) Depressive Disorder Factsheet
National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) Depression Overview

diseases.name: Generalized Anxiety Disorder
diseases.medicalName: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD / Pathological Autonomic Arousal)
diseases.shortDescription: A mental health disorder characterized by persistent, excessive, and uncontrollable worry about a variety of everyday matters.
diseases.whatIsIt: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is diagnosed when an individual experiences chronic, excessive worry and anxiety about multiple life domains (work, health, finances, family) more days than not for at least 6 months. It is accompanied by somatic symptoms of autonomic hyperactivity and muscle tension.
whyDoesItHappen: Hyperactivity of the amygdala and impaired top-down inhibitory regulation from the prefrontal cortex
Dysregulation of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), serotonin, and norepinephrine neurotransmission
Genetic predisposition with family clustering of anxiety and mood disorders
Prolonged environmental stressors, childhood adversity, or personality traits like high neuroticism
signsYouMayNotice: Persistent, uncontrollable worry that is out of proportion to the likelihood or impact of feared events
Restlessness, feeling keyed up, on edge, or unable to relax
Becoming easily fatigued during everyday tasks
Difficulty concentrating or mind going completely blank
Irritability and low frustration tolerance
Chronic muscle tension, especially in neck, shoulders, and jaw (clenching/grinding teeth)
Sleep disturbance: difficulty falling or staying asleep, or restless, unsatisfying sleep
Somatic symptoms: rapid heartbeat, dry mouth, sweating, trembling, nausea, and frequent urination
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable neurobiological and psychological condition.
whoIsAtRisk: Women are twice as likely as men to experience generalized anxiety disorder
Individuals with a personal or family history of anxiety, depression, or substance use disorders
People with chronic medical conditions or high environmental stress
howToReduceRisk: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT): identify and challenge cognitive distortions, catastrophic thinking, and avoidance behaviors
Practice evidence-based relaxation techniques: diaphragmatic breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, and mindfulness
Limit or eliminate caffeine, energy drinks, and nicotine, which directly trigger autonomic nervous system arousal
Take prescribed guideline-directed medications (SSRIs, SNRIs, buspirone) under psychiatric supervision
whenToSeeDoctor: Worry that disrupts your ability to work, maintain relationships, or manage everyday responsibilities
Panic attacks: sudden surges of intense fear with heart palpitations, chest pain, and feeling like you cannot breathe
Using alcohol or non-prescribed substances to cope with feelings of anxiety
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects roughly 300 million people worldwide; anxiety disorders are the most common mental disorders globally.
reliableSources: American Psychiatric Association (APA) DSM-5-TR Generalized Anxiety Disorder
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) Guidelines for GAD
World Health Organization (WHO) Anxiety Disorders Factsheet

diseases.name: Bipolar Disorder
diseases.medicalName: Bipolar Affective Disorder (Type I / Type II Cyclical Mood Episodes)
diseases.shortDescription: A brain disorder that causes unusual shifts in mood, energy, activity levels, and concentration, fluctuating between mania and depression.
diseases.whatIsIt: Bipolar Disorder is a severe cyclical mood condition. Bipolar I is characterized by at least one manic episode (sustained abnormally elevated or irritable mood with grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, and impulsivity). Bipolar II involves recurrent major depressive episodes alternating with hypomanic episodes (less extreme mania without psychosis).
whyDoesItHappen: High genetic heritability (estimated between 70% and 85%), with multiple susceptibility genes influencing synaptic plasticity and calcium signaling
Disruption of circadian rhythms and clock gene regulation governing sleep-wake cycles
Neurochemical imbalances in dopamine, glutamate, serotonin, and intracellular secondary messenger pathways
Triggers: acute sleep deprivation, significant psychological trauma, substance use, or corticosteroid therapy
signsYouMayNotice: Manic episode: feeling euphoric, invulnerable, "on top of the world," or extremely irritable and agitated
Drastically reduced need for sleep (feeling fully rested after only 2 or 3 hours of sleep)
Racing thoughts, rapid pressurized speech that is difficult for others to interrupt
Grandiosity or inflated self-esteem: believing one has special powers, supreme wealth, or a divine mission
High-risk impulsive behaviors: lavish spending sprees, reckless driving, risky business investments, or sexual indiscretions
Depressive episode: profound sadness, loss of interest, lethargy, suicidal ideation, and inability to get out of bed
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable severe neurobiological mood disorder with strong genetic roots.
whoIsAtRisk: Individuals with a first-degree relative (parent or sibling) with bipolar disorder (increases risk up to 10-fold)
Peak age of onset is in late adolescence or early adulthood (ages 15 to 25)
howToReduceRisk: Maintain strict, unvarying daily sleep routines; sleep loss is the most potent trigger for manic episodes
Adhere consistently to prescribed mood stabilizers (lithium, valproate) or second-generation antipsychotics
Avoid illicit stimulants, cocaine, amphetamines, and excessive alcohol
Engage in psychoeducation and Interpersonal and Social Rhythm Therapy (IPSRT)
whenToSeeDoctor: EMERGENCY: Manic behavior that poses immediate danger to oneself or others, or presence of psychotic hallucinations/delusions
Severe depressive episode with active thoughts of self-harm or suicide (call or text 988 immediately)
Drastic shifts in mood and energy recognized by friends, coworkers, or family members
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects approximately 40 million people worldwide; early diagnosis and maintenance treatment are vital to prevent relapse.
reliableSources: CANMAT and ISBD Guidelines for the Management of Patients with Bipolar Disorder
American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder
National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH)

diseases.name: PTSD (Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder)
diseases.shortDescription: A psychiatric disorder that can occur in people who have experienced or witnessed a traumatic event, series of events, or set of circumstances.
diseases.whatIsIt: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) develops following exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence. It is characterized by four symptom clusters: intrusive re-experiencing, persistent avoidance of trauma triggers, negative alterations in cognition/mood, and marked hyperarousal.
whyDoesItHappen: Failure of normal fear extinction learning and memory consolidation in the hippocampus and ventromedial prefrontal cortex
Exaggerated amygdala reactivity to conditioned fear stimuli
Dysregulation of the autonomic nervous system and noradrenergic hyper-reactivity
Severe traumatic events: military combat, sexual assault, physical abuse, severe car accidents, or natural disasters
signsYouMayNotice: Intrusive memories: recurring, involuntary distressing recollections of the trauma
Flashbacks: feeling or acting as though the traumatic event is actually happening again in the present
Distressing, terrifying nightmares about the event
Persistent avoidance of places, people, objects, thoughts, or conversations that recall the trauma
Negative changes in thinking and mood: emotional numbness, persistent guilt, detachment from family, inability to experience joy
Hyperarousal: constant hypervigilance, scanning the environment for threats, exaggerated startle response to sudden noises
Irritability, angry outbursts, sleep disturbance, and reckless or self-destructive behavior
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable trauma-induced neurobiological and psychiatric disorder.
whoIsAtRisk: Military combat veterans, first responders, and emergency medical personnel
Survivors of physical, emotional, or sexual assault or severe domestic violence
Individuals with prior childhood trauma or limited social support following a traumatic event
howToReduceRisk: Access trauma-focused psychotherapies: Prolonged Exposure (PE), Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT), or Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR)
Seek social support from family, support groups, and trusted community members immediately following trauma
Avoid using alcohol or substances to numb emotional distress
whenToSeeDoctor: Trauma symptoms lasting longer than 1 month that impair personal, occupational, or social functioning
Severe intrusive flashbacks or nightmares that prevent restful sleep
Thoughts of self-harm or suicide (call or text 988 immediately)
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Lifetime prevalence is roughly 6% to 8% in the general population, with significantly higher rates in combat veterans and assault survivors.
reliableSources: VA / DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of PTSD
American Psychological Association (APA) Clinical Practice Guideline for PTSD
National Center for PTSD

diseases.name: OCD (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder)
diseases.shortDescription: A long-lasting mental health disorder where a person has uncontrollable, reoccurring thoughts (obsessions) and/or behaviors (compulsions) that they feel the urge to repeat.
diseases.whatIsIt: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is characterized by intrusive, unwanted, anxiety-provoking thoughts, images, or urges (obsessions) that drive the individual to perform repetitive mental or physical acts (compulsions) aimed at reducing distress or preventing a dreaded event, according to rigid rules.
whyDoesItHappen: Dysfunction in the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) neurocircuitry governing habit formation and error detection
Abnormalities in serotonin, dopamine, and glutamate neurotransmitter signaling
Genetic susceptibility with substantial familial heritability
Pediatric Autoimmune Neuropsychiatric Disorders Associated with Streptococcal Infections (PANDAS) in sudden-onset childhood cases
signsYouMayNotice: Common obsessions: intense fear of contamination/germs, fear of harming others accidentally, need for perfect symmetry or order, taboo aggressive or sexual thoughts
Common compulsions: excessive handwashing or cleaning until skin is raw, repeated checking (doors locked, stove off, appliances unplugged)
Mental compulsions: silently repeating words, counting objects, praying, or neutralizing bad thoughts with good ones
Demanding constant reassurance from family members and loved ones
Compulsions consume more than 1 hour per day and cause significant distress and disruption to daily life
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable neurobiological and psychiatric disorder.
whoIsAtRisk: Individuals with a first-degree relative with OCD (increases risk up to 4-fold)
Onset typically occurs during childhood/adolescence (average age 19)
Individuals with high trait perfectionism or anxiety sensitivity
howToReduceRisk: First-line gold standard therapy: Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP), a specialized form of CBT that teaches individuals to tolerate distress without performing rituals
High-dose SSRI medications (fluoxetine, sertraline, fluvoxamine) prescribed under psychiatric guidance
Avoid family accommodation of compulsions (family members answering reassurance questions or participating in cleaning rituals)
whenToSeeDoctor: Obsessive thoughts or repetitive rituals consume more than 1 hour every day
Rituals cause physical harm (e.g. skin breakdown from excessive scrubbing) or severe isolation
Severe anxiety or depressive thoughts triggered by uncontrollable obsessions
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects approximately 1% to 2% of the world’s population (over 100 million individuals).
reliableSources: American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With OCD
International OCD Foundation (IOCDF)
National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) OCD Overview

diseases.name: Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis)
diseases.medicalName: Atopic Dermatitis (Epidermal Barrier Dysregulation & Th2 Inflammation)
diseases.shortDescription: A chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by dry, intensely itchy, and red or inflamed skin patches.
diseases.whatIsIt: Atopic dermatitis is the most common form of eczema. It results from a defect in the epidermal skin barrier (frequently linked to filaggrin gene mutations) combined with an overactive T-helper 2 (Th2) immune response, allowing irritants, microbes, and allergens to penetrate the skin and trigger unrelenting itch-scratch cycles.
whyDoesItHappen: Loss-of-function mutations in the filaggrin (FLG) gene disrupting skin barrier moisture retention
Th2-skewed immune activation releasing pruritogenic cytokines (IL-4, IL-13, IL-31)
Staphylococcus aureus bacterial colonization on disrupted skin perpetuating inflammation
Environmental triggers: dry winter air, harsh soaps, wool fabrics, hot showers, and emotional stress
signsYouMayNotice: Pruritus (intense, persistent itching) that frequently worsens at night, severely disrupting sleep
Dry, red, inflamed patches of skin on the flexural creases (creases of elbows, backs of knees, wrists, neck)
Small, raised bumps that may leak clear fluid and crust over when scratched
Lichenification: thickened, leathery, cracked, and hyperpigmented skin from chronic repeated scratching
Raw, sensitive, swollen skin vulnerable to secondary bacterial infection (honey-colored crusting)
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable chronic inflammatory skin disease; cannot be caught from another person.
whoIsAtRisk: Children (affects up to 20% of children globally, often beginning in infancy)
Individuals with a personal or family history of the "Atopic Triad": eczema, asthma, and allergic rhinitis (hay fever)
howToReduceRisk: Apply thick emollient ointments or creams (ceramide-based) within 3 minutes of bathing to lock in moisture
Take short, lukewarm showers (5 to 10 minutes) and completely avoid harsh, scented antibacterial soaps
Wear soft, breathable, 100% cotton clothing; avoid scratchy wool and synthetic fibers
Use prescribed topical corticosteroids or topical calcineurin inhibitors during acute flares
whenToSeeDoctor: Skin becomes infected: oozing yellow pus, crusting, red streaks, or accompanied by fever
Itching is so severe that it prevents sleep and interferes with school or work performance
Eczema flares fail to respond to over-the-counter moisturizers and hydrocortisone
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects over 230 million people worldwide; one of the most widespread non-fatal skin conditions globally.
reliableSources: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) Guidelines for the Care of Atopic Dermatitis
European Task Force on Atopic Dermatitis (ETFAD)
National Eczema Association

diseases.name: Psoriasis
diseases.shortDescription: A chronic autoimmune disease that speeds up the growth cycle of skin cells, causing thick, red patches covered with silvery scales.
diseases.whatIsIt: Psoriasis is a chronic systemic immune-mediated inflammatory dermatosis. Driven by the IL-23 / IL-17 cytokine immune axis, epidermal keratinocytes proliferate at an accelerated rate (maturing in 3 to 5 days instead of the normal 28 days), accumulating on the skin surface as thick erythematous plaques with silvery scales.
whyDoesItHappen: Dysregulated interaction between dermal dendritic cells, Th17 lymphocytes, and epidermal keratinocytes
Overproduction of inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-23, IL-17A)
Genetic susceptibility involving HLA-Cw6 (PSORS1 locus)
Triggers: streptococcal pharyngitis (triggers guttate psoriasis), skin injury (Koebner phenomenon), stress, smoking, and medications (beta-blockers, lithium)
signsYouMayNotice: Plaque psoriasis: well-demarcated raised, red skin plaques covered with thick, silvery-white micaceous scales
Most commonly located symmetrically on extensor surfaces (outer elbows, knees, scalp, lower back)
Auspitz’s sign: pinpoint bleeding when scales are gently scraped or lifted
Nail psoriasis: pitting (tiny indentations), thickening, yellowish "oil drop" discoloration, or nail lifting (onycholysis)
Itching, burning, or soreness around affected skin plaques
Psoriatic arthritis: swelling and pain in finger joints ("sausage digits" / dactylitis) in up to 30% of patients
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable autoimmune skin and systemic disease; completely non-contagious.
whoIsAtRisk: Adults between 20–35 and 50–60 years of age (bimodal age distribution)
Individuals with a family history of psoriasis
Smokers and individuals with metabolic syndrome or high systemic inflammation
howToReduceRisk: Keep skin hydrated with thick barrier creams and avoid skin cuts, scrapes, and sunburn (which trigger new plaques)
Avoid smoking and heavy alcohol consumption, which reduce treatment efficacy
For moderate-to-severe disease, targeted biologic therapies (anti-IL-17, anti-IL-23) can achieve >90% to 100% skin clearance
whenToSeeDoctor: Joint pain, morning stiffness, or swollen fingers/toes accompanying skin plaques (early psoriatic arthritis)
Plaques covering widespread body surface area (>10%) or involving face and palms
Widespread generalized skin redness and scaling accompanied by fever (erythrodermic psoriasis is a medical emergency)
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects over 125 million people globally (2% to 3% of the world’s population).
reliableSources: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) / National Psoriasis Foundation (NPF) Guidelines
World Health Organization (WHO) Global Report on Psoriasis
International Psoriasis Council

diseases.name: Acne Vulgaris
diseases.medicalName: Acne Vulgaris (Pilosebaceous Follicular Keratinization & C. acnes)
diseases.shortDescription: A common skin condition that occurs when hair follicles become plugged with oil (sebum) and dead skin cells, leading to breakouts.
diseases.whatIsIt: Acne vulgaris is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the pilosebaceous unit. Four key pathogenic factors interact: follicular hyperkeratinization (clogged pores), excess sebum production under androgen control, proliferation of Cutibacterium acnes bacteria, and localized immune inflammation.
whyDoesItHappen: Elevated androgen levels (testosterone/DHEA-S) stimulating sebaceous gland enlargement and sebum overproduction
Abnormal desquamation of follicular keratinocytes creating microcomedones
Proliferation of Cutibacterium acnes within anaerobic sebum-rich follicle environments
Release of pro-inflammatory mediators causing inflammatory papules, pustules, and nodules
signsYouMayNotice: Comedones: open comedones (blackheads: dark surface from oxidized melanin) and closed comedones (whiteheads)
Inflammatory papules (small, red, tender bumps) and pustules (pimples containing white/yellow pus)
Nodules and cysts: large, painful, solid or pus-filled lumps beneath the skin surface that risk deep scarring
Breakouts most prominent on face, forehead, chest, upper back, and shoulders
Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (dark marks left after lesions heal) and atrophic "ice-pick" scarring
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable dermatological condition.
whoIsAtRisk: Adolescents and teenagers (affects over 85% of people aged 12 to 24)
Adult women with hormonal fluctuations (menstrual flares, PCOS)
Individuals using comedogenic cosmetics, heavy pomades, or taking anabolic steroids
howToReduceRisk: Wash face twice daily with a gentle, non-abrasive cleanser; avoid vigorous scrubbing which irritates follicles
Use topical retinoids (adapalene, tretinoin) nightly to prevent follicular pore plugging
Choose non-comedogenic (oil-free) makeup, moisturizers, and sunscreens
Do not pick, squeeze, or pop pimples, which forces bacteria deeper and causes permanent scarring
whenToSeeDoctor: Severe, painful cystic or nodular acne that fails to respond to over-the-counter benzoyl peroxide and salicylic acid
Acne causing visible physical scarring or significant psychological distress and anxiety
Adult women with acne accompanied by excess facial hair, hair loss, or irregular periods (evaluate for PCOS)
diseases.howCommonIsIt: The eighth most prevalent disease globally, affecting approximately 650 million individuals worldwide.
reliableSources: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) Guidelines of Care for the Management of Acne Vulgaris
European Dermatology Forum (EDF) Acne Guidelines
British Association of Dermatologists

diseases.name: Vitiligo
diseases.shortDescription: A long-term autoimmune skin condition in which patches of skin lose their pigment, turning milky-white as melanocytes are destroyed.
diseases.whatIsIt: Vitiligo is an acquired autoimmune disorder characterized by progressive destruction of epidermal melanocytes (pigment-producing cells). Autoreactive CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes target melanocyte antigens, leaving circumscribed, depigmented, amelanotic white macules and patches.
whyDoesItHappen: Autoimmune destruction of functional melanocytes by autoreactive CD8+ T cells via the IFN-gamma / CXCL10 pathway
Intracellular oxidative stress in melanocytes triggering heat shock protein release and innate immune activation
Genetic susceptibility involving genes associated with immune regulation (NLRP1, PTPN22, HLA-A/B)
Triggers: severe sunburn, mechanical friction/trauma (Koebner phenomenon), and acute psychological stress
signsYouMayNotice: Patchy loss of skin color: development of chalky or milky-white flat patches (macules) on the skin
Non-segmental vitiligo (most common): symmetric distribution on hands, fingers, face (around eyes and mouth), wrists, and feet
Segmental vitiligo: unilateral white patches following a dermatomal or blaschkoid distribution
Premature whitening or graying of hair on the scalp, eyelashes, eyebrows, or beard (poliosis)
Loss of color in the mucous membranes lining the inside of the mouth and nose
Depigmented patches burn very easily in sunlight due to the total absence of photoprotective melanin
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable autoimmune skin condition; completely non-contagious.
whoIsAtRisk: Can affect people of any skin tone or age, with peak onset between ages 10 and 30
Individuals with personal or family history of other autoimmune conditions (Hashimoto thyroiditis, Type 1 diabetes, alopecia areata)
howToReduceRisk: Apply broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF 50+) meticulously on white patches to prevent severe sunburn
Avoid repetitive skin friction, tight garments, and skin trauma that induce new lesions (Koebner effect)
Modern therapies: topical JAK inhibitors (ruxolitinib) combined with targeted narrow-band UVB (NB-UVB) phototherapy can stimulate follicular repigmentation
whenToSeeDoctor: Appearance of newly spreading white patches on skin, hair, or mucous membranes
Evaluation for associated autoimmune thyroid disorders with routine TSH screening
Counseling regarding medical repigmentation therapies and psychological support
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects 0.5% to 2% of the world population (an estimated 70 to 100 million individuals).
reliableSources: Vitiligo Global Issues Consensus Conference (VGICC) Guidelines
American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) Vitiligo Practice Resources
Global Vitiligo Foundation

diseases.name: Shingles (Herpes Zoster)
diseases.shortDescription: A viral infection that causes a painful, blistering rash that typically develops in a single stripe or band on one side of the body or face.
diseases.whatIsIt: Shingles (herpes zoster) is caused by the reactivation of the Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV), the same virus that causes chickenpox. After primary chickenpox resolves, VZV lies dormant in dorsal root and cranial sensory nerve ganglia for decades until declining cell-mediated immunity allows it to reactivate and travel down sensory nerves to the skin.
whyDoesItHappen: Reactivation of dormant varicella-zoster virus from sensory nerve ganglia
Age-related decline in VZV-specific T-cell immunity (immunosenescence)
Immunosuppressive conditions (cancer chemotherapy, organ transplantation, systemic corticosteroids, HIV/AIDS)
Severe physical or emotional stress
signsYouMayNotice: Prodromal pain: burning, shooting, tingling, or itching sensations in a localized dermatomal area 2 to 4 days before any rash appears
Erythematous macules and papules that quickly develop into clusters of fluid-filled vesicles (blisters)
Unilateral dermatomal distribution: strictly confined to one side of the body, wrapping around the torso like a belt, or on one side of the face
Blisters break open, ooze, and crust over within 7 to 10 days, clearing completely in 2 to 4 weeks
Postherpetic Neuralgia (PHN): severe, burning, stabbing nerve pain that persists for months or years in the affected area after the rash heals
Herpes zoster ophthalmicus: involvement of the trigeminal ophthalmic branch risking corneal ulceration and permanent vision loss
diseases.howDoesItSpread: You cannot catch shingles from someone who has shingles; however, a person with active shingles blisters can spread VZV to someone who has never had chickenpox or the vaccine, causing chickenpox in that person.
whoIsAtRisk: Anyone who has had chickenpox (over 99% of adults over 50)
Adults aged 50 and older (risk rises sharply past age 50)
Individuals with compromised or weakened immune systems
howToReduceRisk: Receive the recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix): over 90% effective at preventing shingles and postherpetic neuralgia in adults 50 and older (2-dose series)
Start prescription oral antiviral medications (valacyclovir, famciclovir) within 72 hours of rash onset to shorten duration and decrease PHN risk
Keep the rash clean and covered with non-stick sterile bandages until crusted over
whenToSeeDoctor: EMERGENCY: Any shingles rash appearing near the eye, forehead, or tip of the nose (Hutchinson’s sign indicates ocular involvement risking blindness)
Start antiviral medications within 72 hours of the rash appearing for maximum clinical benefit
Severe nerve pain persisting long after the skin rash has fully healed
diseases.howCommonIsIt: 1 in 3 people will develop shingles during their lifetime; approximately 1 million cases occur annually in the United States alone.
reliableSources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Shingles Clinical Overview
Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) Zoster Guidelines
American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) Shingles Resources

diseases.name: Urticaria (Hives & Angioedema)
diseases.medicalName: Acute & Chronic Urticaria (Mast Cell-Mediated Wheals & Angioedema)
diseases.shortDescription: Raised, red, intensely itchy skin welts (hives) that can appear anywhere on the body, often accompanied by deeper swelling (angioedema).
diseases.whatIsIt: Urticaria (hives) is characterized by transient, pruritic erythematous wheals caused by mast cell and basophil degranulation, which releases histamine, prostaglandins, and platelet-activating factor. This causes localized dermal vasodilation and increased vascular permeability. It is acute (<6 weeks) or chronic (>=6 weeks).
whyDoesItHappen: IgE-mediated allergic reactions to foods (nuts, shellfish, eggs, dairy), medications (penicillin, NSAIDs), or insect stings
Viral infections (the most common cause of acute hives in young children)
Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU): autoimmune anti-IgE or anti-FceRI autoantibodies triggering continuous mast cell degranulation
Physical stimuli (inducible urticaria): mechanical friction (dermographism), cold, heat, pressure, vibration, or sunlight
signsYouMayNotice: Wheals: raised, pink, red, or skin-colored welts with a central pale swelling surrounded by an erythematous flare
Intense, severe itching (pruritus) that worsens with heat or scratching
Transient nature: individual wheals appear, change shape, and completely resolve within 24 hours without leaving marks (while new ones appear elsewhere)
Angioedema: deeper swelling under the skin affecting lips, eyelids, tongue, hands, and genitalia; feels painful or burning rather than itchy
Dermographism: scratching the skin produces raised linear hives along the scratch lines
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable allergic, autoimmune, or idiopathic mast cell-mediated reaction.
whoIsAtRisk: Individuals with a personal history of allergies, asthma, or atopic dermatitis
People with underlying autoimmune thyroid conditions (Hashimoto thyroiditis)
Women are twice as likely as men to develop chronic spontaneous urticaria
howToReduceRisk: Identify and strictly avoid known trigger allergens, foods, and NSAID medications
Take modern non-sedating second-generation H1-antihistamines (cetirizine, fexofenadine, bilastine) consistently
For refractory chronic urticaria, biologic therapy (omalizumab / anti-IgE) provides targeted mast cell stabilization
Apply cool compresses and avoid hot baths, tight abrasive clothing, and alcohol during acute flares
whenToSeeDoctor: EMERGENCY: Swelling of the tongue, throat, difficulty breathing, wheezing, or dizziness (signs of anaphylaxis requiring immediate intramuscular epinephrine and 911 / 108)
Hives that persist continuously for more than 6 weeks
Individual hives that are painful, leave purple bruise-like marks (purpura), and last >24 hours (evaluate for urticarial vasculitis)
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Approximately 20% of the population experiences acute urticaria at some point; chronic urticaria affects 1% to 2% of adults.
reliableSources: EAACI / GA2LEN / EuroGuiDerm / APAAACI Guideline for the Definition, Classification, Diagnosis, and Management of Urticaria
American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology (AAAAI)
World Allergy Organization (WAO)

diseases.name: Sickle Cell & Thalassemia
diseases.shortDescription: Inherited genetic blood disorders that affect hemoglobin, causing chronic hemolytic anemia and painful vaso-occlusive crises.
diseases.whatIsIt: Hemoglobinopathies are genetic disorders of hemoglobin. In Sickle Cell Disease (SCD), an abnormal hemoglobin variant (HbS) polymerizes under low oxygen conditions, deforming red blood cells into rigid sickle shapes that obstruct microvessels. In Thalassemia, defective synthesis of alpha or beta globin chains causes ineffective erythropoiesis and severe chronic hemolysis.
whyDoesItHappen: Sickle Cell: autosomal recessive point mutation in the HBB gene (substitution of valine for glutamic acid at codon 6)
Thalassemia: deletions (alpha) or mutations (beta) in globin genes on chromosomes 16 and 11
Vaso-occlusion in sickle cell causing localized tissue ischemia, infarction, and acute chest syndrome
Severe microcytic hypochromic hemolysis in thalassemia requiring lifelong chronic blood transfusions and iron chelation
signsYouMayNotice: Vaso-occlusive pain crises: sudden, excruciating bone and joint pain that lasts hours to days
Chronic severe fatigue, paleness (pallor), and jaundice (yellowing of eyes from red blood cell breakdown)
Dactylitis: painful swelling of the hands and feet in infants (often the first sign of sickle cell)
Frequent bacterial infections due to functional asplenia from micro-infarctions of the spleen
Delayed growth, puberty, and skeletal changes (facial bone marrow expansion in thalassemia)
Acute chest syndrome: fever, chest pain, and severe hypoxia (a life-threatening emergency in sickle cell)
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable inherited genetic blood disorders passed from parents to biological children via Mendelian autosomal recessive inheritance.
whoIsAtRisk: Individuals of African, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and South Asian descent
Children whose biological parents both carry the sickle cell trait or thalassemia trait (25% chance of disease)
howToReduceRisk: Undergo carrier screening and genetic counseling prior to pregnancy
Maintain adequate hydration and avoid extreme cold, dehydration, and high altitudes which trigger sickling crises
Take hydroxyurea to stimulate fetal hemoglobin (HbF) production, reducing sickle cell pain crises and acute chest syndrome
Adhere to regular blood transfusions and daily iron chelation therapy (deferasirox) in severe thalassemia
whenToSeeDoctor: EMERGENCY: Sudden chest pain, fever, and shortness of breath (acute chest syndrome requires emergency hospital care)
Severe pain crisis that cannot be managed with oral analgesics at home
Fever of 101°F (38.5°C) or higher in a person with sickle cell (requires urgent IV antibiotics due to asplenia)
Sudden pallor, enlargement of the spleen, and lethargy (splenic sequestration crisis)
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Over 300,000 babies are born with severe hemoglobin disorders each year worldwide; millions carry protective traits.
reliableSources: American Society of Hematology (ASH) Sickle Cell Disease Guidelines
Thalassemia International Federation (TIF) Guidelines
CDC Sickle Cell Disease Information

diseases.name: Hemophilia
diseases.medicalName: Congenital Hemophilia (Factor VIII / IX Coagulation Deficiency)
diseases.shortDescription: A rare inherited genetic bleeding disorder in which the blood does not clot normally because it lacks sufficient blood-clotting proteins.
diseases.whatIsIt: Hemophilia is an X-linked recessive bleeding disorder caused by mutations in the F8 gene (Hemophilia A: Factor VIII deficiency, 80% of cases) or F9 gene (Hemophilia B: Factor IX deficiency / Christmas disease). Without adequate clotting factor, the coagulation cascade cannot generate a stable secondary fibrin clot.
whyDoesItHappen: Mutations in F8 (Xq28) or F9 (Xq27) genes leading to qualitative or quantitative deficiency of clotting factors VIII or IX
Inability to form intrinsic tenase complex, severely impairing thrombin generation on activated platelet surfaces
X-linked recessive inheritance: primarily affects males, while females are typically asymptomatic carriers
signsYouMayNotice: Hemarthrosis: spontaneous bleeding into large weight-bearing joints (knees, elbows, ankles), causing painful swelling, warmth, and stiffness
Extensive, deep muscle hematomas following minor bumps or intramuscular injections
Prolonged bleeding after cuts, dental procedures, circumcision, or minor surgical operations
Spontaneous nosebleeds (epistaxis) that are difficult to stop and bleeding gums
Blood in urine (hematuria) or stools
Intracranial hemorrhage: unexplained drowsiness, severe headache, neck stiffness, or vomiting after head trauma (leading cause of bleeding death)
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable inherited X-linked recessive genetic disorder. Roughly 30% of cases arise from spontaneous de novo mutations with no family history.
whoIsAtRisk: Males born to carrier mothers (50% chance of inheriting the mutated X chromosome)
Family history of maternal male relatives with severe bleeding disorders
howToReduceRisk: Receive prophylactic factor replacement infusions or non-factor bispecific antibody therapy (emicizumab) to maintain steady hemostasis
Avoid contact sports (football, hockey, boxing); participate in low-impact activities like swimming and golf
Never take aspirin, ibuprofen, or NSAIDs which impair platelet aggregation and worsen bleeding risk
Always wear a medical alert identification bracelet indicating hemophilia and factor status
whenToSeeDoctor: EMERGENCY: Any head injury or blow to the head, even if seemingly minor (immediate factor infusion is mandatory to prevent fatal brain bleed)
Severe pain, heat, and swelling in a joint (joint bleed requires immediate factor replacement to prevent chronic arthropathy)
Uncontrolled bleeding from a wound that does not stop with direct pressure
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Affects approximately 1 in 5,000 live male births for Hemophilia A and 1 in 20,000 for Hemophilia B worldwide.
reliableSources: World Federation of Hemophilia (WFH) Guidelines for the Management of Hemophilia
Medical and Scientific Advisory Council (MASAC) of the National Bleeding Disorders Foundation
CDC Hemophilia Overview

diseases.name: Malignant Melanoma
diseases.shortDescription: The most serious type of skin cancer, developing in the melanocyte pigment cells that give color to your skin.
diseases.whatIsIt: Malignant melanoma is an aggressive cutaneous malignancy arising from pigment-producing melanocytes. While it accounts for only about 1% of all skin cancers, it causes the vast majority of skin cancer deaths due to its high propensity for early lymphatic and hematogenous metastasis.
whyDoesItHappen: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation from sunlight and indoor tanning beds inducing cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and DNA damage
Activating somatic mutations in oncogenes: BRAF (V600E mutation present in ~50%), NRAS, or KIT
Loss-of-function mutations in tumor suppressor genes (CDKN2A / p16)
Intermittent intense sunburns, particularly blistering sunburns during childhood and adolescence
signsYouMayNotice: The ABCDE Rules of Melanoma:
A - Asymmetry: One half of a mole does not match the other half
B - Border: Irregular, scalloped, ragged, or poorly defined edges
C - Color: Varied shades of tan, brown, black, red, white, or blue across the same lesion
D - Diameter: Greater than 6 millimeters (about the size of a pencil eraser), though melanomas can be smaller
E - Evolving: Any change in size, shape, color, elevation, or new symptoms like bleeding, oozing, or itching
The "Ugly Duckling" sign: a mole that looks distinctively different from all other moles on the patient’s body
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable neoplastic malignancy. Spreads via regional lymph nodes and hematogenously to lungs, liver, brain, and bones.
whoIsAtRisk: People with fair skin, light eyes, blond or red hair, and a tendency to freckle and burn easily
Individuals with a high total number of moles (>50) or dysplastic (atypical) nevi
Personal or family history of melanoma (increases risk up to 3-fold)
Users of commercial indoor UV tanning beds
howToReduceRisk: Avoid sun exposure during peak UV hours (10:00 AM to 4:00 PM)
Apply broad-spectrum water-resistant sunscreen (SPF 30 or higher) every 2 hours to all exposed skin
Perform monthly head-to-toe skin self-examinations and seek an annual professional full-body skin exam from a dermatologist
Completely avoid indoor UV tanning beds and sun lamps
whenToSeeDoctor: Any new mole or dark spot that displays one or more ABCDE criteria
A spot that bleeds, oozes, itches, or fails to heal after several weeks
A dark streak beneath a fingernail or toenail (subungual melanoma)
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Over 325,000 new cases are diagnosed globally each year; early surgical excision of thin melanomas has a 5-year survival rate >99%.
reliableSources: National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) Melanoma Guidelines 2026
American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) Melanoma Detection Guidelines
Melanoma Research Foundation

diseases.name: Bladder Cancer
diseases.shortDescription: A cancer that begins in the cells lining the inside of the urinary bladder, commonly signaled by painless blood in the urine.
