diseases.whatIsIt: Bladder cancer is predominantly urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma (>90% of cases), arising from the specialized epithelial lining of the urinary tract. It is classified as non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC, ~75%) or muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC, ~25%), which carries a high risk of systemic metastasis.
whyDoesItHappen: Cigarette smoking: tobacco carcinogens (aromatic amines) are filtered by kidneys and stored in the bladder, directly exposing urothelium (smoking accounts for ~50% of cases)
Occupational exposure to industrial chemicals, benzidine dyes, rubber, and aromatic amines
Chronic bladder urothelial irritation from recurrent urinary tract infections, indwelling catheters, or Schistosoma haematobium parasite infection (squamous cell carcinoma)
Prior pelvic radiation therapy or chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide
signsYouMayNotice: Painless gross hematuria: visible blood in the urine (pink, red, or cola-colored) that may come and go over days or weeks
Microscopic hematuria discovered incidentally on routine urine dipstick or urinalysis
Urinary frequency: needing to urinate much more often than usual
Urinary urgency: sudden, urgent feeling of needing to urinate without delay
Dysuria: painful or burning sensation during urination
Advanced signs: pelvic pain, flank pain (from ureteral obstruction), bone pain, and leg swelling
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable malignant neoplasm. Direct invasion into detrusor muscle, perivesical fat, regional pelvic lymph nodes, and liver/lungs.
whoIsAtRisk: Men (men are 3 to 4 times more likely to develop bladder cancer than women)
Older adults (over 90% of diagnoses occur in people aged 55 and older; median age 73)
Cigarette smokers and industrial chemical factory workers
howToReduceRisk: Quit smoking cigarettes (the single most protective action against bladder cancer)
Wear protective respirators and gloves if working around industrial chemicals and dye manufacturing
Drink plenty of fluids throughout the day to dilute chemical carcinogens and promote frequent bladder emptying
whenToSeeDoctor: Any visible blood in your urine (hematuria), even if it only happens once and disappears
Burning or painful urination when urine culture shows no bacterial infection
New onset of intense urinary urgency and frequency in an older adult
diseases.howCommonIsIt: The 10th most common cancer worldwide, with over 573,000 new cases and 212,000 deaths annually.
reliableSources: National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) Bladder Cancer Guidelines
American Urological Association (AUA) Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer Guidelines
European Association of Urology (EAU) Muscle-invasive and Metastatic Bladder Cancer

diseases.name: Esophageal Cancer
diseases.shortDescription: A serious cancer that starts in the food pipe (esophagus), often causing progressive difficulty swallowing.
diseases.whatIsIt: Esophageal cancer manifests primarily as Esophageal Adenocarcinoma (predominantly in the lower third, arising from Barrett’s esophagus induced by chronic acid reflux) or Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma (predominantly in the upper and middle thirds, linked to tobacco, alcohol, and hot beverage consumption).
whyDoesItHappen: Chronic GERD and Barrett’s esophagus (intestinal metaplasia of esophageal squamous epithelium driving adenocarcinoma)
Heavy tobacco smoking and high alcohol consumption (synergistic risk factors for squamous cell carcinoma)
Obesity: high visceral adiposity promotes hiatal hernia and chronic acid exposure
Drinking very hot beverages (>65°C / 149°F) causing chronic thermal mucosal damage
Achalasia or prior ingestion of caustic lye substances
signsYouMayNotice: Progressive dysphagia: difficulty swallowing that begins with solid foods (meat, bread), progresses to soft foods, and eventually liquids
Unintended, rapid weight loss caused by the physical inability to consume adequate food
Substernal chest pain, burning, pressure, or choking sensations while eating
Persistent hoarseness or chronic cough caused by recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement
Regurgitation of undigested food and worsening chronic acid reflux
Hiccups that do not go away and vomiting blood or dark melena stools in advanced stages
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable gastrointestinal malignancy. Spreads early into rich submucosal lymphatic channels, mediastinal lymph nodes, liver, and lungs.
whoIsAtRisk: Men (men are 3 to 4 times more frequently diagnosed than women)
Individuals with long-standing, untreated GERD and Barrett’s esophagus
Heavy tobacco smokers and regular drinkers of distilled spirits
Adults over age 55 (incidence peaks between ages 60 and 70)
howToReduceRisk: Treat and monitor chronic acid reflux (GERD) with your doctor; undergo periodic endoscopic surveillance if diagnosed with Barrett’s esophagus
Completely avoid tobacco smoking and limit alcohol intake
Maintain a healthy body weight and consume a diet rich in fruits and vegetables
Let very hot teas and beverages cool down before drinking
whenToSeeDoctor: Any difficulty or pain when swallowing food (dysphagia requires prompt upper endoscopy)
Food repeatedly feeling "stuck" in the chest or throat during meals
Unexplained weight loss accompanied by chronic heartburn or hoarseness
diseases.howCommonIsIt: The eighth most common cancer worldwide and the sixth leading cause of cancer mortality, with over 600,000 new cases annually.
reliableSources: NCCN Guidelines for Esophageal and Esophagogastric Junction Cancers 2026
American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ASGE) Barrett’s Esophagus Guidelines
World Health Organization (WHO) International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC)

diseases.name: Endometrial Cancer
diseases.shortDescription: Cancer that arises from the lining of the uterus (endometrium), characterized by abnormal postmenopausal or heavy bleeding.
diseases.whatIsIt: Endometrial cancer is the most common gynecologic malignancy in developed nations. Type I endometrioid adenocarcinoma (~80%) is driven by excess unopposed estrogen stimulation of the endometrium; Type II non-endometrioid carcinomas (serous, clear cell) are estrogen-independent, arise from atrophic endometrium, and are more aggressive.
whyDoesItHappen: Unopposed estrogen stimulation: estrogen drives endometrial proliferation without sufficient progesterone to shed the lining
Obesity: peripheral adipose tissue contains aromatase enzymes that convert androstenedione into estrone (obesity increases risk 3- to 4-fold)
Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) causing chronic anovulation and progesterone deficiency
Nulliparity (never having given birth) and early menarche / late menopause (more lifetime ovulatory cycles)
Tamoxifen therapy used for breast cancer (has weak pro-estrogenic effects on the endometrium)
Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer / HNPCC due to DNA mismatch repair mutations)
signsYouMayNotice: Abnormal vaginal bleeding: any vaginal bleeding or spotting in a postmenopausal woman (the classic red flag present in >90% of cases)
In premenopausal women: abnormally heavy, prolonged menstrual bleeding or bleeding between periods (metrorrhagia)
Unusual watery, pink, or foul-smelling vaginal discharge
Pelvic pain, pressure, or cramping
Difficulty or pain during urination and pain during sexual intercourse
Palpable pelvic mass or unexplained weight loss in advanced stages
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable gynecologic malignancy. Extends through myometrium to cervix, pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes, and peritoneal cavity.
whoIsAtRisk: Postmenopausal women (average age at diagnosis is 60 to 65 years)
Women with obesity, diabetes, or PCOS
Women who took estrogen-only hormone replacement therapy without progesterone
Individuals with Lynch syndrome
howToReduceRisk: Maintain a healthy body weight through balanced nutrition and physical activity
Always combine estrogen with progesterone if taking hormone therapy with an intact uterus
Use combination oral contraceptives (which contain progesterone, reducing endometrial cancer risk by up to 50%)
Seek prompt medical evaluation for any abnormal bleeding; early-stage endometrial cancer detected quickly has a 5-year survival rate >95%
whenToSeeDoctor: ANY vaginal bleeding, spotting, or brownish discharge occurring after menopause (never normal)
Unusually heavy, prolonged periods or bleeding between cycles in women over age 35
Persistent pelvic pain or abnormal watery discharge
diseases.howCommonIsIt: The sixth most common cancer in women globally, with over 417,000 new cases diagnosed each year.
reliableSources: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Uterine Neoplasms
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) Committee Opinion on Endometrial Cancer
Society of Gynecologic Oncology (SGO)

diseases.name: Multiple Myeloma
diseases.shortDescription: A cancer of plasma cells in the bone marrow that causes bone destruction, kidney impairment, and severe anemia.
diseases.whatIsIt: Multiple myeloma is a hematologic malignancy characterized by the clonal proliferation of malignant plasma cells in the bone marrow. These cells overproduce a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein / paraprotein) and stimulate osteoclast bone resorption while suppressing normal bone formation, producing the classic "CRAB" features.
whyDoesItHappen: Primary cytogenetic translocations (e.g., t(11;14), t(4;14)) juxtaposing immunoglobulin heavy chain genes with oncogenes
Progression from Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance (MGUS) and Smoldering Myeloma
Upregulation of RANKL and DKK-1 stimulating osteoclasts and causing punched-out osteolytic bone lesions
Deposition of monoclonal light chains in renal tubules causing myeloma kidney and renal failure
signsYouMayNotice: The "CRAB" Clinical Hallmark Criteria:
C - Calcium elevated: Hypercalcemia causing extreme thirst, frequent urination, nausea, constipation, and confusion
R - Renal impairment: Unexplained kidney failure and elevated creatinine caused by toxic light chains
A - Anemia: Severe normocytic normochromic anemia causing profound weakness, fatigue, and pale skin
B - Bone lesions: Deep, aching bone pain (especially in back, ribs, and hips) and pathological fractures from minor movements
Frequent, severe recurrent bacterial infections (pneumonia, sinusitis) due to suppressed normal immunoglobulins
Hyperviscosity syndrome: blurred vision, dizziness, and headache from thick paraprotein in the blood
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable hematologic bone marrow malignancy; develops multifocally throughout the axial skeleton.
whoIsAtRisk: Adults over age 65 (median age at diagnosis is 69)
Men are approximately 1.5 times more likely to be diagnosed than women
People of African descent have more than twice the incidence compared to Caucasian populations
Individuals with known MGUS (progresses to myeloma at a rate of roughly 1% per year)
howToReduceRisk: Regular medical surveillance with serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) for individuals with known MGUS
Maintain good hydration to protect kidneys from light chain cast nephropathy
Modern therapeutic regimens (triplets/quadruplets combining proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory drugs, and anti-CD38 monoclonal antibodies) have dramatically extended survival
whenToSeeDoctor: Persistent, unexplained bone pain (especially back or rib pain) that does not improve with rest
Unexplained severe anemia and fatigue discovered on routine CBC
Recurrent severe infections or elevated serum protein/calcium levels on routine chemistry panels
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Second most common blood cancer, with over 187,000 new cases diagnosed globally each year.
reliableSources: International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG) Diagnostic Criteria
NCCN Guidelines for Multiple Myeloma 2026
Multiple Myeloma Research Foundation (MMRF)

diseases.name: Lymphoma (Hodgkin & Non-Hodgkin)
diseases.shortDescription: A group of blood cancers that develop in the lymphatic system, causing painless swelling of lymph nodes in the neck, armpits, or groin.
diseases.whatIsIt: Lymphoma is a cancer of the lymphatic system, part of the body’s germ-fighting immune network. It is broadly divided into Hodgkin Lymphoma (characterized pathologically by giant, multinucleated Reed-Sternberg cells, ~10% of cases) and Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL, over 60 diverse subtypes arising from B, T, or NK lymphocytes).
whyDoesItHappen: Malignant transformation of B-cells, T-cells, or NK-cells at various stages of differentiation within lymph nodes
Genetic chromosomal translocations (such as t(14;18) in follicular lymphoma or t(8;14) in Burkitt lymphoma)
Viral infections: Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV), Human T-cell Leukemia Virus (HTLV-1), and Hepatitis C
Chronic bacterial stimulation: Helicobacter pylori driving gastric MALT lymphoma
Immunodeficiency states (HIV/AIDS, post-organ transplant immunosuppression) and autoimmune diseases (Sjögren syndrome, Hashimoto thyroiditis)
signsYouMayNotice: Painless, rubbery enlargement of lymph nodes in the neck, armpits, or groin that does not go away
Systemic "B-Symptoms":
1. Unexplained recurrent fevers above 100.4°F (38°C) without sign of infection
2. Drenching night sweats that require changing nightclothes or bedsheets
3. Unexplained loss of more than 10% of body weight over a 6-month period
Persistent generalized itching (pruritus) without an obvious rash
Severe, unyielding fatigue and loss of appetite
Shortness of breath, persistent cough, or chest pressure from enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes
diseases.howDoesItSpread: Non-communicable lymphatic malignancy. Spreads sequentially (Hodgkin) or non-contiguously (Non-Hodgkin) to distant lymph node chains, spleen, bone marrow, and liver.
whoIsAtRisk: Hodgkin Lymphoma: bimodal age distribution (peaks in young adults aged 15–35 and adults over 55)
Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma: risk increases steadily with age (most common in people over 60)
Individuals with compromised immune systems or chronic autoimmune conditions
People with occupational exposure to certain pesticides and herbicides
howToReduceRisk: Prevent and treat chronic infections linked to lymphoma (eradicate H. pylori, treat Hepatitis C)
Avoid unnecessary exposure to chemical solvents and agricultural pesticides
Seek prompt medical evaluation for any painless enlarged lymph node lasting longer than 4 weeks; early Hodgkin lymphoma has a cure rate exceeding 85% to 90%
whenToSeeDoctor: A painless, swollen lymph node in the neck, armpit, or groin that persists for more than 3 to 4 weeks
Presence of B-symptoms: drenching night sweats, unexplained fevers, and rapid weight loss
Persistent shortness of breath or cough accompanied by neck vein swelling
diseases.howCommonIsIt: Over 620,000 people are diagnosed with lymphoma globally each year, making it one of the top 10 most common cancers.
reliableSources: NCCN Guidelines for Hodgkin Lymphoma and B-Cell Lymphomas 2026
